stem: In the thymic cortex, a double-positive thymocyte's TCR can't bind any of the self-MHC molecules on the epithelial cells. What happens to it?
choices: It edits its receptor and tries again
It becomes a regulatory T cell
It is released as a naive CD8 T cell
ex: Thymocytes go double negative (TCR β then α chain) → double positive (positive selection: weak binding of self-MHC; class I binders become CD8, class II binders CD4) → single positive. Negative selection deletes cells that bind self too strongly.
why: Positive selection rewards weak-to-moderate binding of self-MHC; a TCR that can't bind self-MHC is useless, so the cell gets no survival signal.
Receptor editing is a B-cell rescue; a T cell that fails selection simply dies.
Tregs come from thymocytes that bind self-antigen fairly strongly in the medulla.
Only cells that pass both positive and negative selection leave the thymus.

likely.t: Lymphocyte development and tolerance: positive and negative selection, AIRE, Tregs, anergy

stem:
A 12-year-old girl has had oral thrush on and off since early childhood.
History: low blood calcium from hypoparathyroidism; adrenal insufficiency diagnosed this year
Genetic testing: a mutation in the gene that lets thymic medullary cells display proteins normally made only in other organs
Which gene is it?
ex: Central tolerance in the thymus depends on AIRE, which lets thymocytes be tested against proteins made elsewhere in the body (insulin, parathyroid and adrenal proteins). Without it, self-reactive T cells escape and attack those organs.
why: FOXP3 loss (IPEX) removes Tregs: severe early autoimmunity with diarrhea, eczema and diabetes.
RAG1 loss stops V(D)J recombination and causes severe combined immunodeficiency.
Fas defects block activation-induced cell death, enlarging the lymph nodes and spleen (autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome).

AIRE switches on tissue-restricted self-proteins in the thymus so self-reactive thymocytes can be deleted; its loss causes autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.

likely.t: Lymphocyte development and tolerance: positive and negative selection, AIRE, Tregs, anergy

stem:
Which statements about B cell development are true?
1. Receptor editing in a self-reactive immature B cell replaces its heavy chain.
2. B cells complete their development in the thymus.
3. A pre-B cell tests its new heavy chain by pairing it with a surrogate light chain.
4. Mature naive B cells carry both IgM and IgD on their surface.
ex: Pro-B (heavy chain rearranges) → pre-B (pre-BCR with a surrogate light chain and Igα/Igβ; then the light chain rearranges) → immature B (IgM; tested against self; light-chain editing or deletion) → mature naive B (IgM and IgD). Allelic exclusion gives each B cell one specificity.
why: It includes 1, which is false: receptor editing changes only the light chain; a cell still self-reactive after editing dies by apoptosis.

It includes 2, which is false: B cells develop in the bone marrow; the thymus is where T cells develop. It leaves out 4, which is true: IgM and IgD come from one transcript by alternative splicing; this is the only stage with two isotypes at once.

It includes 2, which is false: B cells develop in the bone marrow; the thymus is where T cells develop. It leaves out 3, which is true: the pre-BCR checks that the heavy chain works and can pair with the signaling proteins Igα and Igβ.

Statements 3 and 4 are true. Statement 1 is false: receptor editing changes only the light chain; a cell still self-reactive after editing dies by apoptosis. Statement 2 is false: B cells develop in the bone marrow; the thymus is where T cells develop.

stem: Which description fits regulatory T cells?
choices: CD8 cells that kill infected cells with perforin and granzymes
CD4 cells that need FoxP3 and suppress with IL-10 and TGF-β
CD4 cells that secrete IL-17 to recruit neutrophils
B cells that switch to IgA in the gut
ex: Peripheral tolerance uses anergy (no costimulation), activation-induced cell death (Fas–FasL), limits on where naive T cells travel, and Tregs (FoxP3+): IL-2 deprivation, IL-10 and TGF-β, APC inhibition and cytotoxicity.
why: That describes cytotoxic T lymphocytes.
Tregs suppress self-reactive cells by secreting IL-10 and TGF-β, using up IL-2, inhibiting APCs and killing; FOXP3 mutation (IPEX) causes severe autoimmunity.
That describes Th17 cells.
IgA-switched B cells are not T cells; TGF-β from Tregs and epithelium does favor IgA switching.

stem: Which statement about immune tolerance is true?
choices: Central tolerance takes place in the lymph nodes and spleen
A naive T cell that meets its antigen without costimulation becomes anergic
Immune-privileged tissues express little Fas ligand so lymphocytes can survive there
B cells are screened more strictly for self-reactivity than T cells are
ex: Central tolerance deletes self-reactive lymphocytes as they develop; peripheral tolerance (anergy, Tregs, activation-induced cell death) handles those that escape. Immune-privileged sites (brain, eye, testes, uterus) add barriers, TGF-β and IL-10, and FasL.
why: Central tolerance happens in the primary lymphoid organs (thymus and bone marrow); peripheral tolerance acts afterward.
This is true: signal 1 without signal 2 leaves the cell unresponsive (anergy, not apoptosis).
They express high FasL, which triggers apoptosis in entering lymphocytes, along with TGF-β and IL-10.
T-cell selection is the stricter: thymocytes must pass positive and negative selection, while B cells can still be refined after leaving the marrow.

stem:
A 58-year-old man's medical history lists rheumatic heart disease after a childhood strep throat.
Which mechanism explains how a throat infection damaged his heart valves?
choices: Epitope spreading after a cardiac catheter injured a valve
An inherited loss of AIRE in the thymus
Immune complexes of strep toxin settling in the valve
Molecular mimicry between streptococcal and heart proteins
ex: Environmental triggers of autoimmunity: molecular mimicry (rheumatic fever), new or hidden epitopes (neoantigens, sequestered cryptic antigens) and epitope spreading (pemphigus vulgaris). Genetic risk comes largely from HLA alleles.
why: Epitope spreading broadens an existing autoimmune response; it doesn't explain the link to a strep infection.
AIRE loss causes autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome, not rheumatic heart disease.
Post-streptococcal immune complexes damage the kidney (glomerulonephritis); rheumatic fever is cross-reactivity.
Streptococcal proteins share short sequences with heart proteins, so the antibacterial response also attacks heart tissue (acute rheumatic fever).

stem: Which HLA allele is most strongly associated with ankylosing spondylitis?
ex: MHC haplotype decides which peptides are presented, so certain alleles predispose to autoimmunity: HLA-B27 (ankylosing spondylitis), HLA-DR4 (rheumatoid arthritis), HLA-DQ2/DQ8 (celiac disease).
why: HLA-B27, an MHC class I allele, is strongly linked to ankylosing spondylitis (association, not proven cause).
HLA-DR4 is linked to rheumatoid arthritis, where citrullinated joint proteins fit its class II groove better.
HLA-DQ2 (and DQ8) are linked to celiac disease.
HLA-A2 is a common class I allele without that link.

stem: True or false: Allergic contact dermatitis to nickel is mediated by IgE on mast cells.
ex: Nickel binds skin proteins and creates neoantigens that sensitized T cells attack 24–72 hours after contact: a type IV reaction, the most common one.
why: Nickel dermatitis is type IV: T cells and macrophages, delayed 1–3 days, with no IgE involved.
Contact dermatitis is T-cell mediated (type IV); IgE and mast cells drive type I reactions such as hives and anaphylaxis.

stem: Each of the following is a type II hypersensitivity reaction EXCEPT:
choices: Hemolytic transfusion reaction to ABO-mismatched blood
Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
Hemolytic anemia from penicillin bound to red cells
ex: Type II = antibody (IgG or IgM) against antigens fixed on cells, destroying them through complement, phagocytosis or ADCC, or blocking their function. Penicillin can cause all four types.
why: Preformed antibodies against the donor's blood-group antigens destroy the transfused red cells (type II).
Maternal anti-RhD IgG crosses the placenta and destroys fetal red cells (type II).
Poison ivy dermatitis is type IV: sensitized T cells react 1–3 days after contact.
The drug on the red-cell surface forms a neoantigen that antibodies target (type II).

stem: Which statement about type I hypersensitivity is false?
choices: During sensitization, Th2 cells and IL-4 drive B cells to switch to IgE
Allergen-specific IgE already sits on mast cell Fc receptors before the second exposure
The late phase, hours after exposure, is driven mainly by preformed histamine
A wheal is fluid leaking into the skin, and the flare is redness from dilated vessels
ex: Immediate phase (within about 30 minutes): preformed mediators such as histamine and proteases. Late phase (4 or more hours): recruited eosinophils and Th2 cells, leukotrienes and prostaglandins, more like ordinary inflammation.
why: This is true: the first exposure generates allergen-specific IgE.
This is true: re-exposure cross-links that IgE and triggers degranulation.

This is the false one: preformed histamine acts in the first minutes; the late phase (4 or more hours) comes from recruited eosinophils (major basic protein) and newly made leukotrienes and prostaglandins.
This is true: the wheal-and-flare is the classic skin sign of a type I reaction.

stem: Which epithelium lines the lung alveoli and the blood vessels, where substances must cross quickly?
ex: Epithelium is named for its layers (simple, stratified, pseudostratified) and the shape of its outermost cells (squamous, cuboidal, columnar), plus transitional epithelium in the urinary tract.
why: A single layer of flat cells gives the shortest diffusion distance: endothelium, mesothelium, alveoli and Bowman's capsule.
Simple cuboidal lines kidney tubules, thyroid follicles and small gland ducts.
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar lines the trachea and bronchi.
Stratified squamous protects against wear (skin, mouth, esophagus); it is too thick for exchange.

likely.t: Epithelium classification and where each type lines the body, oral mucosa included

stem:
A biopsy of healthy attached gingiva is examined under the microscope.
Which epithelium covers it?
ex: Stratified squamous epithelium is keratinized in the epidermis and the masticatory mucosa (gingiva, hard palate) and nonkeratinized in most of the oral lining mucosa, the esophagus and the vagina. New cells come only from the basal layer.
why: Simple columnar lines the stomach and intestines; it can't withstand chewing forces.
This is respiratory epithelium, found in the nasal cavity, trachea and bronchi.
Transitional epithelium is limited to the urinary tract.
Masticatory mucosa (attached gingiva and hard palate) has a keratinized surface layer that resists the friction of chewing.

likely.t: Epithelium classification and where each type lines the body, oral mucosa included

stem: Which junction links the intermediate (keratin) filaments of neighboring cells and is the target of autoantibodies in pemphigus vulgaris?
ex: Tight junction = seal; adherens junction = actin; desmosome = intermediate filaments between cells; hemidesmosome = intermediate filaments to the basal lamina (integrins); gap junction = communication.
why: Tight junctions seal neighboring cells with claudins and occludins and control paracellular passage.
Desmosomes are spot welds of cadherins (such as desmoglein) anchored to intermediate filaments; pemphigus antibodies break them.
Gap junctions are connexon channels that pass ions and small molecules between cells.
The adhesion belt links actin filaments of neighboring cells through cadherins.

likely.t: Cell junctions and the basement membrane: desmosome versus hemidesmosome, avascular epithelium

stem: True or false: Epithelium has no blood vessels of its own and gets nutrients by diffusion from the connective tissue beneath its basement membrane.
ex: Epithelium is avascular. Nutrients and wastes cross the basal lamina between the epithelium and capillaries in the underlying connective tissue.
why: Epithelium is avascular; the basal lamina lets nutrients move from the connective tissue's capillaries to the cells and metabolites move back.
The statement is accurate: epithelium has no vessels and relies on diffusion across the basement membrane.

stem: In an H&E section, which structures stain deep blue-purple with hematoxylin?
choices: Nuclei and other basophilic, acid-rich structures
ex: Hematoxylin stains basophilic structures blue or purple; eosin stains acidophilic structures pink or red; periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stains carbohydrate-rich structures (glycogen, mucus, basement membranes) magenta.
why: Collagen is acidophilic and stains pink with eosin.
Hematoxylin binds acidic (basophilic) material such as DNA in nuclei and RNA in rough ER; mast cell granules stain the same way.
Most cytoplasm is acidophilic and stains pink with eosin.
Red cells are packed with hemoglobin and stain bright pink-red with eosin.

likely.t: Stains, germ layers, gland secretion modes and surface specializations

stem: In holocrine secretion, whole cells break down and are released along with their product. Which gland secretes this way?
ex: Merocrine = exocytosis (most glands, including salivary glands); apocrine = part of the apical cell pinches off; holocrine = the whole cell is shed (sebaceous glands). Exocrine glands secrete into ducts; endocrine glands lose their ducts and secrete into blood.
why: Salivary glands are merocrine: they release their product by exocytosis.
The mammary gland releases its lipid apocrine fashion, pinching off a bit of apical cytoplasm.
Eccrine sweat glands are merocrine.
Sebaceous gland cells fill with lipid and disintegrate to release sebum.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Brown adipose tissue is multilocular and makes heat without shivering.
2. Serum is plasma from which the clotting factors have been removed.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: White fat is unilocular (one big droplet) and stores energy and makes leptin; brown fat is multilocular, rich in mitochondria, uncouples with thermogenin to make heat, and is most plentiful at birth. Serum is what is left after blood clots.
why: Statement 1 is true: its many small droplets and mitochondria use thermogenin (UCP1) to uncouple oxidation from ATP synthesis; it is most plentiful at birth. Statement 2 is true: blood that clots leaves serum; plasma from unclotted blood still holds fibrinogen and the other clotting factors.

Statement 1 is true, not false: its many small droplets and mitochondria use thermogenin (UCP1) to uncouple oxidation from ATP synthesis; it is most plentiful at birth. Statement 2 is true, not false: blood that clots leaves serum; plasma from unclotted blood still holds fibrinogen and the other clotting factors.
Statement 2 is true, not false: blood that clots leaves serum; plasma from unclotted blood still holds fibrinogen and the other clotting factors.
Statement 1 is true, not false: its many small droplets and mitochondria use thermogenin (UCP1) to uncouple oxidation from ATP synthesis; it is most plentiful at birth.

likely.t: Connective tissue: resident versus transient cells, collagen types, adipose and blood

stem: Which statement about the basement membrane is true?
choices: Its lamina densa is a network built on type IV collagen
It is made mainly of type I collagen secreted by osteoblasts
It lies along the apical surface of epithelial cells
It contains the capillaries that feed the epithelium
ex: The basement membrane (basal lamina + reticular lamina) binds epithelium to connective tissue and filters what passes between blood and the cells. PAS stains it.
why: This is true: the basal lamina is lamina lucida (laminin) plus lamina densa (type IV collagen), and reticular fibers lie beneath it.
Type I is the collagen of bone, dentin, skin and tendon; the basal lamina uses type IV collagen and laminin.
It lies under the basal surface and attaches the epithelium to the connective tissue.
It has no vessels; nutrients diffuse across it from capillaries in the connective tissue.

stem:
Which statements about germ layer derivatives are true?
1. The epidermis comes from ectoderm.
2. The liver comes from mesoderm.
3. The kidneys come from mesoderm.
4. The thyroid comes from endoderm.
ex: Ectoderm: nervous tissue, epidermis and sensory placodes. Mesoderm: connective tissue, bone, muscle, heart, kidneys, blood and gonads. Endoderm: the lining of the gut and airways, lungs, liver, pancreas and thyroid.
why: It includes 2, which is false: the liver comes from endoderm, with the gut lining, lungs, pancreas and thyroid. It leaves out 3, which is true: the middle germ layer forms the kidneys along with connective tissue, muscle, the heart, blood and gonads.
It leaves out 4, which is true: the thyroid buds from the endoderm of the embryonic pharynx.
Statements 1, 3 and 4 are true. Statement 2 is false: the liver comes from endoderm, with the gut lining, lungs, pancreas and thyroid.
It leaves out 1, which is true: the outer germ layer forms the epidermis and its derivatives along with nervous tissue.

stem: True or false: Microvilli have a 9+2 microtubule core and beat to move mucus across the surface.
ex: Microvilli are short, still projections with an actin core that increase absorptive surface (the brush border). Motile cilia have the 9+2 microtubule axoneme anchored in a basal body and move mucus or fluid. Stereocilia are long microvilli (epididymis, inner ear).
why: Microvilli have an actin core and don't move; the 9+2 microtubule axoneme belongs to motile cilia.
Cilia, not microvilli, have 9+2 microtubules and beat; microvilli are actin-cored and still.

stem: Which epithelium lines the urinary bladder and flattens as the bladder fills?
ex: Transitional epithelium is found only in the urinary tract; its cells look rounded when relaxed and flatter when distended.
why: Stratified cuboidal epithelium lines sweat gland ducts.
Simple columnar epithelium lines the stomach, intestines and gallbladder.
Its surface cells are rounded when the bladder is relaxed and flatten when it stretches; it lines the ureters, bladder and part of the urethra.
Pseudostratified columnar lines the airways and parts of the male reproductive tract.

stem: Each of the following is a resident cell of connective tissue EXCEPT:
ex: Connective tissue cells are resident (fibroblasts, adipocytes, pericytes, resident macrophages, mast cells) or transient (white blood cells and plasma cells that arrive as needed). They come from mesenchymal or hematopoietic stem cells.
why: Fibroblasts, the main resident cell, make the fibers and ground substance and divide again to heal wounds.
Fat cells are permanent residents of connective tissue.
Neutrophils are transient: they leave the blood only when inflammation calls them in.
Pericytes wrap capillaries and help repair damaged capillary beds.

stem: Reticular fibers, the fine supporting mesh of lymph nodes, spleen and bone marrow, are made of which collagen?
ex: Extracellular matrix = fibers (collagen, elastic, reticular) + ground substance (glycosaminoglycans, proteoglycans, adhesive glycoproteins such as fibronectin). Elastic fibers are elastin cross-linked covalently on a fibrillin scaffold.
why: Reticular fibers are type III collagen, held by the reticular cells that secrete them.
Type I, the most abundant collagen, is in bone, dentin, skin, tendon and ligament.
Type II is the collagen of cartilage.
Type IV forms the lamina densa of the basal lamina.

stem:
A 58-year-old man is evaluated before extractions.
History: myocardial infarction 4 months ago, hypertension, 40 pack-years of smoking
Medications: aspirin, metoprolol, atorvastatin
The dentist reviews how the infarcted heart muscle looked in the first days after the infarct. Which pattern of necrosis was present?
ex: Coagulative necrosis is the pattern of infarcts in every solid organ except the brain. The architecture is kept, and the dead cells are eosinophilic with no nuclei.
why: An infarct of a solid organ other than the brain keeps its outlines: pink cells without nuclei.
Liquefactive necrosis is the pattern of a brain infarct or an abscess, where enzymes digest the tissue.
Caseous necrosis is the cheese-like center of a TB granuloma.
Fat necrosis comes from lipases, as in acute pancreatitis.

likely.t: Necrosis patterns and the organ or disease each belongs to (coagulative infarct, liquefactive brain and abscess, caseous TB, fat necrosis pancreas, fibrinoid vessels)

stem:
Which pairings of necrosis pattern and setting are correct?
1. Coagulative necrosis: a kidney infarct
2. Liquefactive necrosis: a brain infarct
3. Caseous necrosis: acute pancreatitis
4. Fibrinoid necrosis: malignant hypertension
ex: Coagulative: infarcts outside the brain. Liquefactive: brain infarcts and abscesses. Caseous: TB. Fat necrosis: pancreatitis. Fibrinoid: vessel walls in malignant hypertension or immune-complex disease.
why: It leaves out 4, which is true: fibrin-like material in damaged vessel walls is seen in malignant hypertension and immune-complex vasculitis.
Statements 1, 2 and 4 are true. Statement 3 is false: acute pancreatitis causes fat necrosis; caseous necrosis is the pattern of tuberculosis.

It leaves out 2, which is true: the brain has little stroma, so its infarcts liquefy. It includes 3, which is false: acute pancreatitis causes fat necrosis; caseous necrosis is the pattern of tuberculosis.

It leaves out 1, which is true: infarcts of solid organs other than the brain are coagulative. It includes 3, which is false: acute pancreatitis causes fat necrosis; caseous necrosis is the pattern of tuberculosis.

likely.t: Necrosis patterns and the organ or disease each belongs to (coagulative infarct, liquefactive brain and abscess, caseous TB, fat necrosis pancreas, fibrinoid vessels)

stem: True or false: Apoptosis, like necrosis, sets off an inflammatory response around the dying cell.
ex: Apoptosis shrinks the cell into membrane-bound apoptotic bodies that are eaten quietly, with no inflammation. Necrosis spills the cell's contents and always brings inflammation.
why: Only necrosis spills cell contents and brings inflammation; apoptosis doesn't.
Apoptotic bodies are cleared without inflammation, which is one of the main differences from necrosis.

likely.t: Apoptosis versus necrosis, and the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. In the intrinsic pathway of apoptosis, cytochrome c leaks from the mitochondria once BCL2 is blocked.
2. The extrinsic pathway starts when Fas on a cytotoxic T cell binds Fas ligand on the target cell.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Intrinsic: BCL2 blocked, cytochrome c out, caspases on. Extrinsic: FasL on the cytotoxic T cell crosslinks Fas on the target, adaptor proteins bind the death domain, caspases on. Both end in caspases.
why: Statement 2 is false, not true: it is the other way around: Fas ligand on the T cell binds Fas (the death receptor) on the target cell.
Statement 1 is true, not false: loss of survival signals or DNA damage blocks BCL2, mitochondrial channels open and cytochrome c activates the caspases.

Statement 1 is true: loss of survival signals or DNA damage blocks BCL2, mitochondrial channels open and cytochrome c activates the caspases. Statement 2 is false: it is the other way around: Fas ligand on the T cell binds Fas (the death receptor) on the target cell.

Statement 1 is true, not false: loss of survival signals or DNA damage blocks BCL2, mitochondrial channels open and cytochrome c activates the caspases. Statement 2 is false, not true: it is the other way around: Fas ligand on the T cell binds Fas (the death receptor) on the target cell.

likely.t: Apoptosis versus necrosis, and the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways

stem:
A 62-year-old woman with a chronic cough has a bronchial biopsy.
History: 45 pack-years, still smoking
Findings: the normal ciliated columnar lining is replaced by stratified squamous epithelium; no atypia
Which adaptation is this?
ex: Squamous metaplasia in a smoker's bronchus is the classic example. The squamous lining resists smoke but loses the cilia and mucus, and metaplasia can go on to dysplasia and cancer.
why: Dysplasia is disordered, atypical growth; this biopsy shows no atypia.
One adult cell type (ciliated columnar) is replaced by another (squamous), through reprogrammed stem cells.
Hyperplasia is more cells of the same type.
Hypertrophy is bigger cells of the same type.

stem: Which statement about pathologic calcification is true?
choices: Dystrophic calcification needs a raised serum calcium to form
Calcium in an atherosclerotic plaque is an example of metastatic calcification
Metastatic calcification affects normal tissues when serum calcium is high
Metastatic calcification is limited to necrotic tissue such as old infarcts
ex: Dystrophic: normal blood calcium, damaged tissue (atheroma, old valves, necrosis). Metastatic: high blood calcium, normal tissue.
why: Dystrophic calcification happens with a normal serum calcium.
A plaque is damaged tissue, so its calcium is dystrophic.
Hypercalcemia (hyperparathyroidism, bone destruction, vitamin D excess, kidney failure) deposits calcium in normal vessels, kidneys, lungs and stomach.
Calcium in necrotic or damaged tissue is dystrophic; metastatic calcium lands in normal tissue.

stem: Each step of leukocyte recruitment is paired with the molecules that drive it EXCEPT:
ex: Rolling (selectins) → firm adhesion (integrins) → transmigration (PECAM-1) → chemotaxis (chemokines).
why: Integrins on the leukocyte bind ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 on the endothelium to stop it.
PECAM-1 (CD31) lets the leukocyte squeeze between endothelial cells.
Chemokines, C5a, leukotriene B4 and bacterial products set the gradient it follows.
Rolling is driven by selectins; integrins come in at the next step.

likely.t: Acute inflammation: exudate, leukocyte recruitment steps; chronic inflammation: M1 and M2 macrophages

stem: True or false: An exudate is rich in protein and cells and is the fluid typical of inflammation.
ex: Leaky vessels in inflammation let protein and cells out: exudate (pus if it is full of neutrophils). A transudate is low in protein and cells and comes from raised hydrostatic or lowered oncotic pressure.
why: Inflamed vessels leak protein and cells, so the fluid is an exudate.
The low-protein, cell-poor fluid is the transudate; inflammation makes exudate.

stem: In a healing wound, macrophages are switched on by IL-4 and IL-13. What do these macrophages mainly do?
choices: Secrete IL-10 and TGF-β to promote repair
Make reactive oxygen species and nitric oxide to kill microbes
Secrete IL-12 and TNF to drive inflammation
ex: M1 (classical, IFN-γ): warriors that make ROS, NO, IL-1, TNF, IL-6, IL-12. M2 (alternative, IL-4 and IL-13): healers that make IL-10 and TGF-β.
why: IL-4 and IL-13 make alternative (M2) macrophages, the healers: IL-10 and TGF-β calm inflammation and bring new vessels, fibroblasts and collagen.
Killing with ROS and NO is the job of classical (M1) macrophages, switched on by IFN-γ and microbial products.
IL-12 and TNF come from pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages.
Histamine is released by mast cells, not macrophages.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman asks about a lump on her earlobe.
History: ears pierced 18 months ago
Findings: a firm, shiny, raised scar that has kept growing and now extends well beyond the original piercing; no signs of infection
What is this lesion?
ex: Both keloids and hypertrophic scars come from too much collagen. The keloid crosses the wound boundary and doesn't regress; the hypertrophic scar stays inside it and can regress.
why: A hypertrophic scar is raised but stays within the wound and can regress.
A keloid grows beyond the edges of the original wound and does not regress.
Exuberant granulation is excess granulation tissue standing above the wound surface while it heals.
A contracture is excessive shrinking of a wound that deforms it.

likely.t: Repair and scar problems (granulation tissue, keloid versus hypertrophic scar) and acute-phase proteins

stem: Which statement about tissue repair is false?
choices: Neurons and heart muscle are permanent cells, so their injuries heal by scar
Vitamin C deficiency and steroids both weaken the healing scar
Granulation tissue is made mostly of dense, mature collagen
Healing by second intention needs more granulation tissue and contraction
ex: Repair runs from a platelet plug, to inflammation with granulation tissue (vessels and fibroblasts, little collagen), to remodeling, where collagen gives the scar its strength.
why: This is true: permanent cells can't divide, so the gap fills with scar.
This is true: vitamin C is needed to make collagen, and steroids cut fibrosis and TGF-β.
This is the false one: granulation tissue is new small vessels, fibroblasts and macrophages with little collagen; collagen builds up later, in remodeling.
This is true: a large gap fills from below with more granulation tissue and myofibroblast contraction.

stem: Which acute-phase protein causes the anemia of chronic disease?
ex: The liver makes the acute-phase proteins in response to IL-6 and other cytokines: CRP, fibrinogen, serum amyloid A and hepcidin.
why: CRP is an opsonin that binds complement and marks heart-attack risk.
Fibrinogen makes red cells stack and raises the sedimentation rate.
Serum amyloid A is an opsonin; long exposure causes secondary amyloidosis.
Hepcidin traps iron in stores, so less is available to make red cells.

stem: Which tumor is malignant even though its name ends in -oma?
ex: Benign tumors end in -oma. Lymphoma, melanoma, mesothelioma, seminoma and hepatoma are malignant despite the ending.
why: Melanoma is a malignant tumor of melanocytes, one of the names that break the -oma rule.
A lipoma is a benign tumor of fat.
A chondroma is a benign tumor of cartilage; its malignant form is chondrosarcoma.
A papilloma is a benign epithelial tumor with finger-like projections.

likely.t: Tumor naming, benign versus malignant, grade versus stage

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. A tumor's grade describes how far it has spread, using the TNM system.
2. Stage predicts prognosis better than grade.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Grade: how differentiated the cells look. Stage: the extent of disease by TNM. Stage matters more for prognosis.
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: grade is the degree of differentiation under the microscope (1 = well differentiated); spread is the stage.
Statement 2 is true, not false: stage (tumor size, nodes, distant metastasis; AJCC I-IV) is the stronger predictor.

Statement 1 is false, not true: grade is the degree of differentiation under the microscope (1 = well differentiated); spread is the stage. Statement 2 is true, not false: stage (tumor size, nodes, distant metastasis; AJCC I-IV) is the stronger predictor.

Statement 1 is false: grade is the degree of differentiation under the microscope (1 = well differentiated); spread is the stage. Statement 2 is true: stage (tumor size, nodes, distant metastasis; AJCC I-IV) is the stronger predictor.

stem: True or false: A malignant tumor of epithelium is a carcinoma, and a malignant tumor of mesenchymal tissue is a sarcoma.
ex: Carcinomas (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma) come from epithelium; sarcomas (fibrosarcoma, chondrosarcoma) come from connective tissue.
why: Epithelium gives carcinomas; mesenchyme gives sarcomas.
The pairing is right as written: carcinoma is epithelial, sarcoma is mesenchymal.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has a mass removed from her mandible. Each of the following findings would favor malignancy EXCEPT:
choices: Spread to the submandibular lymph nodes
A fibrous capsule around well-differentiated cells
ex: Benign: well differentiated, slow, encapsulated, never metastasizes. Malignant: anaplastic, often fast, invasive, metastasizes.
why: Metastasis is the hallmark of malignancy.
A capsule and well-differentiated cells are features of a benign tumor.
Anaplasia (bizarre nuclei, atypical mitoses, lost polarity) points to malignancy.
Invasion of neighboring tissue is a feature of malignancy.

stem: Which enzyme protects cells by removing free radicals?
ex: Oxidative stress is radicals made faster than they are removed. Removal: superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase.
why: NADPH oxidase makes superoxide for the neutrophil's respiratory burst.
Cytochrome P450 turns some toxins into reactive metabolites that generate radicals.
Superoxide dismutase, with catalase and glutathione peroxidase, clears free radicals.
Myeloperoxidase makes hypochlorous acid to kill microbes; it doesn't clear radicals.

stem:
A 32-year-old woman has a painful cluster of small ulcers on her hard palate.
History: local anesthetic injection there 2 days ago; she gets "cold sores" on her lip a few times a year
Findings: coalescing 1-2 mm ulcers on the keratinized palatal mucosa; no fever
Where does the virus responsible stay latent between episodes?
ex: HSV-1 infects mucosal epithelium and travels up the sensory nerve to hide in the trigeminal ganglion. Stress, sunlight or trauma (an injection) can reactivate it.
why: B cells are where EBV and HHV-8 stay latent.
Recurrent intraoral herpes (HSV-1) on keratinized mucosa, set off by trauma; HSV-1 is latent in the trigeminal ganglion.
Sacral ganglia are the usual latency site of HSV-2 (genital herpes).
Monocytes are a latency site of CMV.

likely.t: Human herpesviruses HHV-1 to HHV-8: diseases and latency sites, with their oral lesions

stem:
A 41-year-old man comes for a cleaning.
History: HIV infection, not taking his medications
Labs: CD4 count 150/µL
Findings: white, corrugated vertical folds on both lateral borders of the tongue that don't wipe off; painless
Which virus causes this lesion?
ex: Oral hairy leukoplakia (lateral tongue, doesn't wipe off) is a classic oral sign of HIV, caused by EBV. Candidiasis wipes off; Kaposi sarcoma is HHV-8.
why: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, a red-purple lesion often on the palate or gingiva.
HPV-16 is linked to oropharyngeal carcinoma; low-risk HPV types cause oral warts.
Oral hairy leukoplakia is EBV replicating in the tongue's epithelium of an immunosuppressed patient.
CMV causes retinitis and other disease in AIDS but not hairy leukoplakia.

likely.t: Human herpesviruses HHV-1 to HHV-8: diseases and latency sites, with their oral lesions

stem:
Which pairings of herpesvirus and disease are correct?
1. HHV-3: shingles along one dermatome
2. HHV-5: Kaposi sarcoma
3. HHV-4: infectious mononucleosis
4. HHV-6: roseola
ex: HHV-1 and 2: HSV. HHV-3: VZV. HHV-4: EBV. HHV-5: CMV. HHV-6 and 7: roseola. HHV-8: Kaposi sarcoma.
why: It includes 2, which is false: HHV-5 is cytomegalovirus; Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8.
It leaves out 4, which is true: HHV-6 (and HHV-7) cause roseola in young children.
Statements 1, 3 and 4 are true. Statement 2 is false: HHV-5 is cytomegalovirus; Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8.
It leaves out 1, which is true: varicella-zoster virus reactivates from a sensory ganglion as shingles. It includes 2, which is false: HHV-5 is cytomegalovirus; Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8.

stem:
A 23-year-old dental student has titers drawn before clinic.
History: three-dose hepatitis B series in childhood; no known exposures
Labs: HBsAg negative; anti-HBs positive; anti-HBc negative
What do these results show?
choices: Immunity from a past natural infection
Acute infection in the window period
ex: Anti-HBs alone = vaccinated. Anti-HBs + anti-HBc = recovered. HBsAg + IgM anti-HBc = acute. HBsAg + IgG anti-HBc for over 6 months = chronic.
why: Recovery from infection leaves both anti-HBs and anti-HBc.
Chronic infection shows HBsAg (over 6 months) with anti-HBc and no anti-HBs.
The window period shows IgM anti-HBc alone, with HBsAg already gone and anti-HBs not yet present.
The vaccine contains only surface antigen, so it makes anti-HBs and never anti-HBc.

likely.t: Hepatitis A to E (spread, chronicity, prevention) and hepatitis B serology

stem: Which statement about the hepatitis viruses is false?
choices: Hepatitis C is the only hepatitis virus with a DNA genome
Hepatitis D can infect only a person who also carries hepatitis B
Hepatitis E spreads by the fecal-oral route and is most dangerous in pregnancy
Hepatitis A is a picornavirus that never causes a chronic infection
ex: Only HBV is a DNA virus. A and E are fecal-oral and acute; B, C and D are bloodborne and can become chronic.
why: This is the false one: hepatitis B (a hepadnavirus) is the DNA virus; hepatitis C is a (+)RNA flavivirus.
This is true: HDV is defective and borrows the HBV surface antigen for its coat (coinfection or superinfection).
This is true: HEV comes from contaminated water or undercooked meat, with about 20% mortality in pregnant women.
This is true: HAV is a naked (+)RNA picornavirus and is always self-limited.

likely.t: Hepatitis A to E (spread, chronicity, prevention) and hepatitis B serology

stem: True or false: An infant infected with hepatitis B at birth is far more likely to develop chronic infection than an infected adult.
ex: About 90% of infants infected at birth become chronic carriers, compared with about 5% of adults. That is why the vaccine series starts at birth.
why: Chronic infection follows in about 90% of infected newborns and about 5% of infected adults.
The risk really is much higher in newborns (about 90%) than in adults (about 5%).

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Antigenic shift happens only in influenza A and comes from swapped genome segments.
2. Neuraminidase frees new virions by cleaving sialic acid, and oseltamivir blocks it.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true

stem:
A 6-year-old boy is brought in with fever.
History: not vaccinated; 3 days of cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes
Findings: tiny blue-white spots on a red base on the buccal mucosa opposite the molars; no rash yet
What is the most likely cause?
ex: Measles (a paramyxovirus with H and F glycoproteins) is extremely contagious and infectious before symptoms. Koplik spots are seen only in measles. MMR is a live attenuated vaccine.
why: Coxsackie A causes herpangina: vesicles and ulcers on the soft palate and tonsillar pillars.
Cough, coryza and conjunctivitis with Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa are measles; the spots come before the rash.
Parvovirus B19 causes fifth disease, with slapped cheeks and a lacy rash.
VZV causes chickenpox, with crops of itchy vesicles in different stages.

stem: True or false: AIDS is defined by a CD4 count below 200 cells/µL or an AIDS-defining illness.
ex: Above 500 is usually symptom-free; 200-500 brings early symptoms; below 200 is AIDS. Untreated, it takes 5-10 years in adults.
why: Below 200 CD4 cells/µL is severe immunosuppression, which defines AIDS.
The cutoff is right: below 200/µL (or an AIDS-defining illness) is AIDS.

likely.t: HIV: entry through CD4 and CCR5 or CXCR4, the life cycle, stages by CD4 count and tests

stem: A patient had a high-risk exposure to HIV 10 days ago and has a fever and rash. Which test is most sensitive this early?
ex: Antibody (and antigen-antibody) tests screen; plasma HIV RNA is the most sensitive and also tracks treatment; CD4 counts stage the disease.
why: Antibodies take weeks to appear, so the test can be negative now.
The CD4 count stages the disease; it doesn't diagnose infection.
Viral RNA in plasma is the most sensitive and precise test and turns positive first.
p24 needs a lot of antigen in the blood to be detected, so it is less sensitive than RNA.

stem: Which statement about the HIV-1 life cycle is true?
choices: Integrase copies the RNA genome into DNA
Protease inhibitors stop the virus from binding to CD4
The virus is fully infectious as soon as it buds from the cell
gp120 binds CD4 and then a coreceptor, CCR5 or CXCR4
ex: Attach (gp120 to CD4 and CCR5 or CXCR4) → fuse (gp41) → reverse transcriptase → integrase → host RNA polymerase II → bud → protease matures it.
why: Reverse transcriptase makes the DNA copy; integrase inserts it into the host chromosome.
Protease inhibitors block the cutting of Gag after budding, so the virus can't mature.
A budded particle is immature; protease must cut Gag before it becomes infectious.
CD4 binding plus a chemokine coreceptor lets gp41 fuse the envelope with the cell.

stem: Each of these viruses uses reverse transcriptase EXCEPT:
ex: Reverse transcriptase is used by the retroviruses (HIV, HTLV-1) and by hepatitis B.
why: HCV is a (+)RNA flavivirus that copies its RNA with an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and never makes DNA.
HIV-1 is a retrovirus (Baltimore class VI).
HBV (class VII) copies its DNA genome through an RNA step with reverse transcriptase.
HTLV-1 is a retrovirus, like HIV.

stem: True or false: Enveloped viruses resist drying, acid and detergents better than naked viruses.
ex: The lipid envelope is fragile, so enveloped viruses need to stay wet and are spread by blood, sex or droplets. Naked capsids survive drying and the gut, which is why HAV and polio spread fecal-orally.
why: It is the naked viruses that are hardier; the envelope is easily destroyed by drying, acid and detergent.
Naked capsids are the tough ones; enveloped viruses are disrupted by drying, acid, detergents and solvents.

stem: A 54-year-old man has an HPV-16-positive carcinoma at the base of his tongue. How does the viral E7 protein push the cells to divide?
choices: It tags p53 for destruction through E6AP
It binds Rb, which frees E2F to start S phase
It inserts next to MYC as in Burkitt lymphoma
It blocks apoptosis through the HBx protein
ex: High-risk HPV (16, 18) infects basal epithelial cells. E6 removes p53; E7 inactivates Rb. HPV causes more than 30% of oropharyngeal cancers.
why: That is E6: with E6AP it ubiquitinates p53, which is then degraded.
E7 binds the tumor suppressor Rb, releasing the E2F transcription factor that drives G1 to S.
MYC translocation is the mechanism of Burkitt lymphoma, linked to EBV.
HBx is a hepatitis B protein, not an HPV one.

likely.t: Oncogenic viruses: HPV E6 and E7, EBV, HBV and HCV, HTLV-1, HHV-8

stem: A man is bitten on the hand by a bat. How would rabies virus reach his brain?
choices: By a primary viremia in the bloodstream
In infected B cells crossing into the brain
By retrograde axonal transport in nerves
By lymphatic spread to the cervical nodes
ex: Bite → muscle → motor neurons → spinal cord and dorsal root ganglia → brain by fast retrograde transport. Negri bodies (nucleocapsids in neurons) are diagnostic. The long incubation lets post-exposure vaccine work.
why: Rabies doesn't rely on viremia; it travels inside neurons.
B cells carry EBV, not rabies.
Rabies replicates slowly in muscle at the bite, enters motor nerve endings and climbs the axons to the spinal cord and brain.
Lymphatic spread isn't how rabies reaches the central nervous system.

stem: Each virus is correctly paired with a cancer it causes EXCEPT:
ex: EBV: lymphomas, nasopharyngeal carcinoma. HPV 16 and 18: cervical, oropharyngeal. HBV and HCV: liver. HTLV-1: adult T-cell leukemia. HHV-8: Kaposi sarcoma.
why: EBV causes nasopharyngeal and gastric carcinoma and B-cell lymphomas.
About half of hepatocellular carcinomas are linked to HBV.
High-risk HPV causes cervical and oropharyngeal carcinomas.
HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma; Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8.

stem:
A 4-year-old girl has a fever and refuses to eat.
Findings: small vesicles and shallow ulcers on the soft palate, uvula and tonsillar pillars; gingiva and lips normal; similar cases at her daycare
The virus responsible belongs to which group?
ex: Coxsackie A causes herpangina and hand-foot-and-mouth disease. Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis involves the gingiva and the front of the mouth.
why: Herpangina (posterior mouth, sparing the gingiva) is caused by coxsackie A, a picornavirus.
Primary herpes (HSV-1) causes ulcers all over, with swollen, red gingiva.
Paramyxoviruses include measles and mumps; measles gives Koplik spots, not posterior ulcers.
HPV causes papillomas and warts, not acute vesicles.

stem:
A 52-year-old man is a new patient.
History: injection drug use in his twenties; anti-HCV positive and HCV RNA positive on screening
Findings: normal oral exam; ALT mildly raised
Which statement about his infection is correct?
choices: A booster of the hepatitis C vaccine will clear it
Direct-acting antivirals can cure over 95% of cases
Hepatitis C immune globulin is the main treatment
Most people who are infected clear the virus without treatment
ex: HCV: bloodborne (+)RNA flavivirus, chronic in about 85%, a leading cause of cirrhosis and liver cancer, no vaccine or immune globulin, cured by direct-acting antivirals. Adults are screened once.
why: There is no hepatitis C vaccine.
8-12 weeks of direct-acting antivirals cures more than 95% of HCV infections and lowers the risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer.
There is no immune globulin for hepatitis C.
Only about 15% clear it; about 85% become chronic.

stem: In a gram stain, which step separates gram-positive from gram-negative bacteria?
ex: Crystal violet, iodine, alcohol, safranin. Thick peptidoglycan keeps the purple (gram-positive); thin peptidoglycan with an outer membrane loses it and turns pink (gram-negative).
why: Crystal violet stains every cell purple at first.
Iodine fixes the violet in every cell.
Alcohol washes the violet out of thin gram-negative walls but not out of thick gram-positive ones.
Safranin only colors the cells that were decolorized; the difference is already made.

likely.t: Gram-positive versus gram-negative envelope and the gram stain

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Gram-positive bacteria have an outer membrane with porins.
2. Endospores are formed mainly by gram-negative cocci.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan, teichoic acids, one membrane; some rods form spores. Gram-negative: thin peptidoglycan, outer membrane with LPS and porins, no spores.
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: the outer membrane, porins and LPS belong to gram-negative bacteria; gram-positives have one membrane and a thick wall. Statement 2 is false, not true: spores are made by gram-positive rods, Bacillus and Clostridium.

stem: True or false: Exotoxins are proteins that can be made into toxoid vaccines, while endotoxin can't.
ex: Exotoxins are strongly antigenic proteins, so inactivated forms (toxoids, such as tetanus) make protective vaccines. Endotoxin is lipid A, weakly antigenic, with no toxoid.
why: Exotoxins are antigenic proteins (tetanus toxoid); endotoxin (lipid A) is poorly antigenic.
It is right as written: toxoids exist only for protein exotoxins.

likely.t: Exotoxins versus endotoxin and the classic toxins (cholera, Shiga, tetanus, botulinum, staph)

stem:
Seven people at a church lunch start vomiting about 3 hours after eating.
History: they shared a custard dessert left out for several hours; one food handler has a bandaged, crusted cut on her hand
Findings: forceful vomiting and cramps; no fever; all recover within a day
What is the most likely cause?
ex: S. aureus enterotoxins A-E are heat-stable and acid-resistant and cause vomiting. The bacteria come from a carrier's skin or nose into food left warm.
why: C. perfringens food poisoning is mostly watery diarrhea about half a day after eating meat dishes.
Salmonella has to grow in the gut first, so it takes longer and usually brings fever and diarrhea.
Cholera causes massive watery diarrhea, typically from contaminated water or shellfish.
Heat-stable staph enterotoxin is already in the food, so vomiting starts within hours with no fever.

likely.t: Exotoxins versus endotoxin and the classic toxins (cholera, Shiga, tetanus, botulinum, staph)

stem:
A 55-year-old man has a boil drained from his neck.
Lab: gram-positive cocci in clusters; catalase-positive; coagulase-positive; resistant to oxacillin and methicillin
What explains the methicillin resistance?
choices: mecA, which codes for the altered binding protein PBP2a
A β-lactamase that hydrolyzes the drug
An efflux pump in its outer membrane that exports the drug
Loss of its peptidoglycan cell wall
ex: Penicillin resistance: β-lactamase. Methicillin resistance (MRSA): mecA makes PBP2a, a different mechanism. Treat MRSA with vancomycin, and drain the abscess.
why: PBP2a has low affinity for β-lactams, so it keeps cross-linking the wall; that is MRSA, treated with vancomycin.
β-lactamase is how about 90% of strains resist penicillin; methicillin was made to resist it.
S. aureus is gram-positive and has no outer membrane.
Staphylococci keep their wall; wall-less bacteria are mycoplasmas.

likely.t: S. aureus virulence, abscess and MRSA; S. epidermidis biofilm; S. pneumoniae capsule

stem: Which statement about the staphylococci is true?
choices: S. aureus is catalase-negative, unlike the streptococci
S. epidermidis is coagulase-negative and colonizes implants through biofilm
Protein A of S. aureus coats it with antibody and so speeds its phagocytosis
Staphylococci grow in chains, while streptococci grow in clusters
ex: Staph: clusters, catalase-positive. S. aureus: coagulase-positive, protein A, leukocidin, abscesses. S. epidermidis: coagulase-negative, biofilm on devices.
why: Staphylococci are catalase-positive; streptococci are catalase-negative.
S. epidermidis, normal skin flora, causes infections of catheters, prosthetic joints and valves through biofilm.
Protein A binds the Fc end of antibody, which blocks opsonization and phagocytosis.
It is the reverse: staphylococci form clusters, streptococci form chains.

stem:
A 70-year-old woman is admitted with pneumonia.
Vitals: temperature 39.6 °C, respiratory rate 28
Chest x-ray: consolidation of the right lower lobe
Sputum gram stain: gram-positive, lancet-shaped diplococci
Which virulence factor mainly lets this organism avoid phagocytosis?
ex: S. pneumoniae is the leading cause of community-acquired pneumonia, often after a viral respiratory infection: lobar consolidation, high fever, productive cough.
why: Protein A belongs to S. aureus.
Teichoic acid helps gram-positives stick and stirs inflammation, but it doesn't block phagocytosis.
S. pneumoniae's thick capsule resists phagocytosis and complement; vaccines are made against capsule types.
Coagulase is an S. aureus enzyme that builds fibrin around it.

stem: Each toxin is correctly paired with its action EXCEPT:
choices: Cholera toxin: raises cAMP, causing watery diarrhea
Shiga toxin: stops protein synthesis in host cells and can lead to kidney failure
Exfoliative toxin: splits the epidermis, causing scalded skin
Tetanus toxin: blocks acetylcholine release, causing flaccid paralysis
ex: Botulinum: no acetylcholine, flaccid. Tetanus: no inhibition, spastic (lockjaw). Cholera: cAMP, watery diarrhea. Shiga: protein synthesis, HUS.
why: Cholera toxin drives chloride and water into the gut lumen.
Shiga toxin of EHEC O157:H7 causes bloody diarrhea and hemolytic uremic syndrome.
S. aureus exfoliative toxins break the desmosomes between epidermal cells.
Tetanus toxin blocks the release of inhibitory transmitters (GABA, glycine) and causes spastic paralysis; blocking acetylcholine is botulinum toxin.

stem:
Which statements about gene transfer between bacteria are true?
1. Transformation is the uptake of naked DNA by a competent cell.
2. Transduction moves bacterial DNA inside a bacteriophage.
3. Conjugation needs a sex pilus from an F+ donor.
4. Generalized transduction moves only the genes beside the prophage's insertion site.
ex: Transformation (naked DNA), transduction (phage; generalized = random, specialized = beside the prophage), conjugation (sex pilus, F+ to F−). Plasmids spread resistance and toxin genes.
why: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are true. Statement 4 is false: that describes specialized transduction; generalized transduction packages random fragments of the chromosome.
It includes 4, which is false: that describes specialized transduction; generalized transduction packages random fragments of the chromosome.

It leaves out 3, which is true: the donor's pilus contacts the recipient and one plasmid strand passes across. It includes 4, which is false: that describes specialized transduction; generalized transduction packages random fragments of the chromosome.

It leaves out 1, which is true: Griffith's pneumococci gained a capsule gene from free DNA this way. It includes 4, which is false: that describes specialized transduction; generalized transduction packages random fragments of the chromosome.

likely.t: Gene transfer, growth curve and the three ways to make ATP

stem:
A 22-year-old woman has a painful red eye.
History: sleeps in her soft contact lenses
Findings: a corneal ulcer with discharge
Lab: gram-negative rod, oxidase-positive, does not ferment lactose, blue-green pigment
What is the most likely organism?
ex: Pseudomonas: opportunist, nosocomial, multidrug-resistant; cystic fibrosis, burns, ventilators and long-wear contact lenses.
why: Pseudomonas is the leading cause of contact-lens keratitis: an aerobic, non-fermenting gram-negative rod.
Klebsiella ferments lactose and causes pneumonia, sepsis and UTI.
E. coli ferments lactose and is a gut organism.
N. gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative diplococcus, not a rod; it causes conjunctivitis, especially in newborns.

likely.t: Gram-negative rods, MacConkey agar and the periodontal red complex

stem: True or false: Bacteria divide most rapidly during the stationary phase of the growth curve.
ex: Lag (adjusting), log (exponential division; antibiotics work best), stationary (division equals death as nutrients run out), death.
why: The fastest division is in the log (exponential) phase; in the stationary phase growth and death balance.
Growth is fastest in the log phase; the stationary phase is a plateau.

stem: Which pathway uses nitrate, sulfate or fumarate as the final electron acceptor?
ex: Every route starts with glycolysis. Aerobic: O2, most ATP. Anaerobic respiration: another acceptor, less ATP. Fermentation: 2 ATP.
why: Fermentation uses no electron transport chain; pyruvate itself is reduced to regenerate NAD+.
Anaerobic respiration runs the TCA cycle and electron transport chain but ends on a molecule other than oxygen.
Aerobic respiration ends on molecular oxygen.
Glycolysis makes pyruvate, ATP and NADH; it has no final electron acceptor of its own.

stem: Which statement about gram-negative pathogens is false?
choices: Helicobacter pylori is a helical, microaerophilic rod linked to ulcers and gastric cancer
EHEC O157:H7 makes Shiga toxin and can cause hemolytic uremic syndrome
Klebsiella pneumoniae forms pale, non-fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar
Vibrio cholerae is a comma-shaped rod whose toxin causes watery diarrhea
ex: MacConkey agar grows only gram-negatives: lactose fermenters (E. coli, Klebsiella) pink, non-fermenters (Pseudomonas, Salmonella) pale.
why: This is true: its flagella take it through the stomach mucus.
This is true: Shiga toxin stops protein synthesis and damages vessels and kidneys.
This is the false one: Klebsiella ferments lactose and grows as pink, mucoid colonies; pale colonies are non-fermenters such as Pseudomonas.
This is true: cholera toxin causes secretory diarrhea, treated with fluids and electrolytes.

stem: A 50-year-old man has generalized severe periodontitis with deep bleeding pockets. Which three species form the red complex?
choices: Fusobacterium nucleatum, Prevotella melaninogenica and Veillonella parvula
Staphylococcus aureus, S. epidermidis, Streptococcus pyogenes
Porphyromonas gingivalis, Tannerella forsythia, Treponema denticola
ex: Chronic periodontitis is caused by gram-negative subgingival anaerobes; the red complex marks severe disease. T. denticola damages tissue with proteases and hydrogen sulfide.
why: These are caries-associated gram-positive bacteria.
These are oral anaerobes found in mixed infections, but they aren't the red complex.
These gram-positive cocci aren't the organisms of chronic periodontitis.
These gram-negative anaerobes are found together in severe periodontitis.

stem: Why is Streptococcus mutans so important in dental caries?
choices: It makes acid, tolerates acid and builds glucans from sucrose
It forms endospores that resist fluoride
Its lipid A dissolves enamel crystals
It is an obligate aerobe that lives mainly on the dorsum of the tongue
ex: Caries is a sugar-driven biofilm disease. S. mutans (with lactobacilli and others) ferments sugar to lactic acid; with C. albicans the acid output, and caries, increase.
why: S. mutans is acidogenic and aciduric (down to about pH 4.4), and its glucosyltransferases turn sucrose into sticky glucans for the biofilm.
Streptococci don't form spores.
Lipid A is gram-negative endotoxin; S. mutans is gram-positive, and it is acid that dissolves enamel.
Streptococci are facultative anaerobes, and S. mutans lives in plaque on teeth.

stem: True or false: Bacteria make their ATP at the plasma membrane, since they have no mitochondria.
ex: The respiratory chain sits in the bacterial plasma membrane, which is also negatively charged and so a target for cationic antimicrobial peptides.
why: With no mitochondria, the electron transport chain lies in the plasma membrane.
It is right: bacteria have no mitochondria, and their membrane does the job.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Endotoxin is released mainly when gram-negative bacteria lyse.
2. Endotoxin is heat-labile and strongly antigenic.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Endotoxin: lipid A of gram-negative LPS, stable, low toxicity per gram, poorly antigenic, causes fever and septic shock. Exotoxins: proteins, mostly labile, very potent, toxoids.
why: Statement 2 is false, not true: endotoxin is heat-stable and weakly antigenic; heat-labile, strongly antigenic toxins are the protein exotoxins.
Statement 1 is true, not false: lipid A is part of the outer membrane and is freed when the cell is broken by the immune response or antibiotics.

stem:
A 72-year-old woman has a burning mouth.
History: asthma, wears a complete upper denture day and night
Medications: inhaled fluticasone-salmeterol
Findings: white curd-like plaques on the palate and buccal mucosa that wipe off, leaving a red, raw base
The usual antifungals act on which molecule of the causative organism?
ex: Candida is a commensal that causes thrush when defenses drop: inhaled steroids (rinse after use), dentures, antibiotics, diabetes, dry mouth, HIV.
why: Cholesterol is the human membrane sterol, which is why amphotericin's weaker binding to it causes toxicity.
Chitin is in the fungal wall, but the common antifungals aren't aimed at it (echinocandins act on glucan).
Peptidoglycan is a bacterial wall polymer; fungi don't have it.
This is oral candidiasis. Polyenes (nystatin, amphotericin B) bind ergosterol and azoles block its synthesis.

likely.t: Fungi: ergosterol, dimorphism, endemic mycoses by region, Candida and the vessel-invading molds

stem:
A 48-year-old man has a dry cough and fever for 3 weeks.
History: explores caves in Missouri; lives near the Mississippi River
Chest x-ray: patchy infiltrates with enlarged hilar lymph nodes
Biopsy: small oval yeasts packed inside macrophages, with granulomas
What is the most likely organism?
ex: Histoplasmosis is usually mild or silent; heavy exposure can cause severe pneumonia, and spread is rare except in the immunosuppressed. Macrophages engulf it and CD4 T cells clear it; itraconazole treats it.
why: Bat or bird droppings in the Ohio and Mississippi valleys, and small yeasts inside macrophages, are Histoplasma.
Coccidioides is endemic to the Southwest desert (valley fever) and forms spherules.
Aspergillus grows as septate hyphae, mostly in neutropenic or allergic patients.
Candida is an opportunist that rarely causes pneumonia in a healthy man.

likely.t: Fungi: ergosterol, dimorphism, endemic mycoses by region, Candida and the vessel-invading molds

stem:
A 55-year-old man is admitted with facial pain and swelling.
History: type 1 diabetes, now in ketoacidosis
Findings: a black, necrotic area on the hard palate; nasal discharge
Biopsy: broad, ribbon-like hyphae without septa, branching at right angles, invading blood vessels
What is the most likely cause?
ex: Mucor and Rhizopus invade vessels, causing thrombosis, infarction and black necrosis; ketoacidosis is the classic risk. It is an emergency.
why: Aspergillus also invades vessels, but its hyphae are narrow, septate and branch at acute angles.
Broad, aseptate hyphae at right angles invading vessels in a patient in ketoacidosis are mucormycosis (rhinocerebral form).
Candida forms yeasts and pseudohyphae and rarely causes black palatal necrosis.
Histoplasma is a small yeast inside macrophages.

stem: True or false: Thermally dimorphic fungi such as Blastomyces grow as molds in the environment and as yeasts at body temperature.
ex: The endemic (true) fungal pathogens are thermally dimorphic: mold in the soil, yeast in the body. Most opportunists aren't.
why: Mold in the cold soil, yeast at 37 °C in the body.
It is right as written: the switch is from mold outside to yeast inside the body.

stem: Which statement about the levels of fungal infection is true?
choices: Sporotrichosis is a superficial mycosis of the outer skin only
Tinea versicolor is a subcutaneous mycosis entering through a thorn prick
Dermatophytes cause cutaneous mycoses because they digest keratin
Coccidioidomycosis is an opportunist seen only in people with AIDS
ex: Superficial (tinea versicolor), cutaneous (dermatophytes), subcutaneous (sporotrichosis), systemic (endemic and opportunistic).
why: Sporotrichosis is subcutaneous: it enters deeper tissue after trauma such as a thorn prick.
Tinea versicolor is superficial and mostly cosmetic.
Dermatophytes are keratinophilic and keratinolytic, so they infect skin, hair and nails (ringworm, athlete's foot).
Coccidioides is an endemic true pathogen that infects healthy people in the Southwest.

stem:
A 45-year-old man has a cough for 6 weeks.
History: moved from a country where TB is common; night sweats; 6 kg weight loss
Chest x-ray: a cavity in the right upper lobe
Sputum: acid-fast rods
What lesion forms in his lung?
choices: Fibrinoid necrosis of small vessel walls
Diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes
ex: M. tuberculosis blocks phagolysosome maturation and grows in macrophages until CD4 T cells' IFN-γ activates them. The granulomatous, caseating reaction is the hallmark.
why: A neutrophil abscess is the suppurative reaction of pyogenic bacteria such as S. aureus.
Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in vessel walls in immune-complex vasculitis and malignant hypertension.
Diffuse alveolar damage is the lung lesion of severe COVID-19 and other causes of ARDS.
TB drives a Th1 response; IFN-γ-activated macrophages and giant cells wall it off with cheese-like central necrosis.

likely.t: Tuberculosis: airborne spread, the caseating granuloma and why treatment takes months

stem:
Which statements explain why tuberculosis needs months of treatment with several drugs?
1. Bacilli inside granulomas are hard for drugs to reach.
2. The mycobacterial envelope is fluid and highly permeable.
3. Slow-growing, drug-tolerant persisters survive short courses.
4. Any single drug quickly selects resistant mutants.
ex: Granulomas, a poorly permeable lipid envelope, drug-tolerant persisters and the rise of resistance all make TB treatment long and multi-drug. Penicillins don't work at all.
why: It includes 2, which is false: the waxy, mycolic-acid envelope has very low fluidity and permeability, which gives intrinsic drug resistance.

It includes 2, which is false: the waxy, mycolic-acid envelope has very low fluidity and permeability, which gives intrinsic drug resistance. It leaves out 3, which is true: persisters are tolerant of drugs that only kill actively growing cells.
It leaves out 4, which is true: streptomycin alone stopped working within a year, so drugs are combined.
Statements 1, 3 and 4 are true. Statement 2 is false: the waxy, mycolic-acid envelope has very low fluidity and permeability, which gives intrinsic drug resistance.

likely.t: Tuberculosis: airborne spread, the caseating granuloma and why treatment takes months

stem: True or false: Nontuberculous mycobacteria are mostly spread from person to person by coughing.
ex: Nontuberculous mycobacteria live in soil and water and are picked up from the environment. They are rising, hard to treat and a special problem in cystic fibrosis.
why: They come from the environment; person-to-person airborne spread is the pattern of M. tuberculosis.
They are acquired from soil and water, not from other people.

stem:
A 34-year-old man returns 5 weeks after a mandibular third molar extraction.
Findings: a firm, painless swelling over the angle of the jaw with several draining sinus tracts; the pus contains tiny yellow granules
Which describes the organism and its treatment?
choices: A gram-positive branching anaerobe; a long course of penicillin
An acid-fast aerobe; months of four-drug therapy
A gram-negative diplococcus; one dose of ceftriaxone
A dimorphic fungus; a course of itraconazole
ex: Actinomyces is oral flora that invades after extraction or trauma; it is slow-growing, hard to culture and forms molar-tooth colonies.
why: Cervicofacial actinomycosis (Actinomyces israelii): sinus tracts with sulfur granules that cross tissue planes, treated with drainage and long-term penicillin.
That is tuberculosis; oral TB is usually a chronic ulcer, not draining tracts with granules.
That describes N. gonorrhoeae, a sexually transmitted infection.
Actinomyces was once mistaken for a fungus because of its branching filaments, but it is a bacterium.

likely.t: Anaerobes: clues, sampling and the key organisms (Actinomyces, Fusobacterium, Clostridium toxins)

stem:
A 17-year-old girl had a sore throat a week ago.
Now: high fever, a tender swelling along the side of her neck, and cough with chest pain
Imaging: thrombosis of the internal jugular vein; scattered nodules in both lungs
Which organism is most likely?
ex: Fusobacteria are gram-negative anaerobic rods of the mouth. Lemierre syndrome is more common in adolescents and has a high mortality.
why: S. pyogenes causes pharyngitis but isn't the agent of Lemierre syndrome.
Lemierre syndrome: a strep-throat-like illness followed by septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein and septic lung emboli.
B. fragilis lives in the colon and causes abdominal abscesses.

It forms spores in the alveoli
The organism has no cell wall

Start amoxicillin, as he is under 12
Give supportive care only, as it is viral
ex: R. rickettsii infects endothelium, causing vasculitis, a petechial rash spreading from the wrists and ankles to the palms and soles, and possibly DIC. About 23% die untreated.

N. gonorrhoeae has a polysaccharide capsule, like N. meningitidis
Reinfection with gonorrhea is common because its pili change their antigens
People without a spleen are at higher risk of fulminant meningococcal sepsis
ex: Both are gram-negative diplococci found only in humans. Gonococcus: sexual, no capsule, variable pili, ceftriaxone. Meningococcus: droplets, capsule, vaccine, antibiotics at once.
why: This is true: meningococcemia brings hemorrhagic skin lesions and septic shock.

stem: A scraping from the base of a lip vesicle shows multinucleated giant cells with nuclear inclusions. Which tissue reaction to infection is this?

stem: Drug A relieves pain with an EC50 of 2 mg and reaches 60% of the maximal possible effect. Drug B has an EC50 of 20 mg and reaches 100%. Which statement compares them correctly?
choices: Drug A is more potent; drug B is more efficacious
Drug B is more potent and more efficacious
Drug A is more potent and more efficacious
They are equally efficacious because both relieve pain
ex: Potency is how much drug is needed (EC50: the lower, the more potent). Efficacy is the most a drug can do (Emax). Clinically, efficacy usually matters more: a less potent drug can still give more relief.
why: Potency is read from the EC50 (A needs a tenth of the dose for half its effect); efficacy is the maximal effect, and B reaches 100%.
B has the higher maximal effect, so it is more efficacious, but its EC50 is ten times higher, so it is less potent.

stem: A second drug moves an agonist's dose-response curve to the right, but a high enough agonist dose still reaches the same maximal effect. What is the second drug?
choices: A physiologic antagonist working through another receptor
ex: Competitive (reversible, same site): right shift, same Emax, surmountable. Irreversible or allosteric noncompetitive: Emax falls and more agonist doesn't fix it (unless spare receptors remain). Physiologic antagonists act on a different receptor with the opposite effect; chemical antagonists bind the drug itself (protamine and heparin).
why: It takes receptors out of play for good, so once spare receptors are used up the maximal effect falls and more agonist can't overcome it.

Binding at a different site keeps the agonist from fully activating the receptor, so Emax falls rather than the curve simply shifting.

why: Statement 2 is false, not true: an inverse agonist has negative intrinsic activity: it lowers the receptor's baseline (constitutive) activity, while a neutral antagonist has none and only blocks.

stem: True or false: The clinical therapeutic index is TD50 divided by ED50, and a drug with a small index, such as warfarin or lithium, needs closer monitoring.
ex: TI = TD50/ED50 (LD50/ED50 in animal studies). The bigger it is, the wider the margin between the effective and the toxic dose. Warfarin, lithium, digoxin and phenytoin are the classic narrow-index drugs.
why: Toxic dose over effective dose is the ratio, and the closer the two doses, the smaller the index: warfarin, lithium and digoxin are the classic narrow-index drugs that need levels or monitoring (INR for warfarin).
Both parts hold: the ratio is toxic dose over effective dose, and narrow-index drugs need levels or monitoring.

stem: Which receptor type sits inside the cell, changes gene transcription and takes hours or days to show its effect?
ex: Fastest to slowest: ligand-gated ion channels (milliseconds), G protein-coupled receptors (seconds), enzyme-linked receptors such as tyrosine kinases (minutes to hours), nuclear receptors (hours to days). Nuclear receptors are the only family not in the cell membrane.
why: The fastest family: binding opens a channel in milliseconds, and it sits in the cell membrane.

stem:
A patient needs a drug at a target plasma concentration of 4 mg/L right away.
Volume of distribution: 50 L
Clearance: 5 L/h
What loading dose is needed?
ex: Loading dose = Vd × target concentration (it fills the volume quickly). Maintenance dose rate = CL × target steady-state concentration (it replaces what is cleared). Here 200 mg loads and 20 mg/h maintains.
why: That is clearance × concentration (5 L/h × 4 mg/L), the maintenance rate in mg per hour, not the loading dose.
That divides the volume by the concentration, which doesn't give a dose.

stem: A drug with a half-life of 8 hours is started at a fixed dose every 8 hours. About when does it reach steady state?
choices: After the first dose, in 8 hours
It depends mainly on the size of each dose
ex: Time to steady state, and time to wash a drug out after stopping, is about 4–5 half-lives. A loading dose is how you reach the target sooner.
why: Steady state takes about 4–5 half-lives: 4–5 × 8 h = 32–40 h, whatever the dose.
One half-life only gets halfway to steady state.
Two half-lives reach about 75% of steady state, not the plateau.
The dose sets how high the plateau is, not how long it takes to get there; the time depends on the half-life.

stem: Which change lengthens a drug's elimination half-life?
choices: Higher renal clearance from improved kidney function
A larger Vd with no change in clearance
A larger dose of a drug with first-order kinetics
Switching the same drug from oral to IV dosing
ex: t½ = 0.693 × Vd / CL. A bigger volume of distribution or a lower clearance (kidney or liver disease) lengthens it; that is why maintenance doses come down in organ failure.
why: More clearance shortens the half-life.
t½ = 0.693 × Vd / CL: more of the drug sits in tissue, so less is in the plasma for the liver and kidney to clear each hour.

stem:
Which statements about bioavailability are true?
1. An IV dose has a bioavailability of 100%.
2. First-pass metabolism in the gut wall and liver lowers oral bioavailability.
3. Sublingual nitroglycerin avoids most first-pass metabolism.
4. Bioavailability measures how fast a drug is absorbed rather than how much reaches the circulation.
ex: Bioavailability (F) is the fraction of a dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged: the extent, not the rate. IV is 100% by definition; oral drugs lose some to first-pass metabolism; sublingual, transdermal and inhaled routes avoid most of it.
why: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are true. Statement 4 is false: bioavailability is the extent, the fraction of the dose that arrives unchanged; how fast it arrives is a separate property (Tmax).

stem:
A 16-year-old is brought in after swallowing a large amount of aspirin, a weak acid.
Findings: ringing in the ears, rapid breathing, vomiting
Which measure speeds the kidneys' removal of the salicylate?
choices: Acidifying the urine with ammonium chloride
Giving naloxone to reverse the fast breathing
ex: Only the un-ionized form crosses membranes. A weak acid is un-ionized in acid and ionized in alkaline fluid, so alkalinizing the urine traps aspirin or phenobarbital in the tubule (ion trapping). The same idea explains why local anesthetics, weak bases, work poorly in an acidic abscess.
why: Acid urine keeps a weak acid un-ionized, so it is reabsorbed; acidifying traps weak bases, not acids.

stem:
An 80-year-old woman taking warfarin bruises easily this month.
History: malnutrition after a long illness
Labs: serum albumin 2.4 g/dL (low); INR 3.8
Medications: warfarin, same dose for a year
What best explains the stronger warfarin effect?
choices: Warfarin binds α1-acid glycoprotein instead and becomes more potent
Low albumin induces CYP2C9 and makes an active metabolite
The albumin-bound fraction is the active form of the drug
More warfarin is unbound, and only free drug is active
ex: Only free drug acts. Albumin binds mainly acidic drugs (warfarin, NSAIDs); α1-acid glycoprotein binds basic drugs (local anesthetics). Low albumin (liver disease, malnutrition, old age) or a second highly bound drug raises the free fraction.
why: α1-acid glycoprotein carries mainly basic drugs (lidocaine); warfarin is an acid carried by albumin, and binding never makes a drug more potent.
Induction would lower warfarin's effect, and its CYP2C9 metabolites are inactive.
Bound drug is a reservoir: it can't cross membranes, act, be filtered or be metabolized until it is released.

stem: A drug is removed at a constant 10 mg per hour whatever its plasma level. Which statement fits?
choices: It follows zero-order kinetics, as ethanol does
Its half-life stays the same as the level falls
It follows first-order kinetics, like most drugs
Doubling the dose will exactly double the steady-state level
ex: First-order: a constant fraction per unit time, constant half-life (most drugs). Zero-order: a constant amount per unit time because elimination is saturated (ethanol, phenytoin, high-dose aspirin).
why: A constant amount per hour means the enzymes are saturated; ethanol, phenytoin and high-dose aspirin behave this way.
A constant half-life is the mark of first-order kinetics; in zero-order kinetics the half-life shortens as the level falls.
First-order kinetics removes a constant fraction (say 10% an hour), so the amount removed falls with the level.
That proportion holds for first-order drugs; with saturated elimination a small dose increase can raise levels much more.

Codeine is an active drug that CYP2D6 converts to an inactive product
Phase II reactions attach a polar group such as glucuronic acid
Cytochrome P450 enzymes sit mainly in hepatocyte mitochondria

Acetaminophen blocks the absorption of codeine
She makes too much morphine and became tolerant
She converts little codeine to morphine
ex: CYP2D6 is highly polymorphic. Poor metabolizers get little relief from codeine (and tramadol); ultrarapid metabolizers make too much morphine and risk respiratory depression, which is why codeine is contraindicated in children under 12. Ibuprofen with acetaminophen avoids the problem.

stem: A man exposed to an organophosphate nerve agent is brought to the emergency department. Which group of findings do you expect?
choices: Dilated pupils, hot dry skin and urinary retention
Dilated pupils, fast pulse, high blood pressure and sweating
Pinpoint pupils, slow pulse, wheezing and heavy secretions
Pinpoint pupils with slow breathing and no secretions
ex: Organophosphates (malathion, parathion, sarin) block acetylcholinesterase irreversibly: DUMBBELSS plus nicotinic effects (fasciculations, paralysis). Atropine blocks the muscarinic effects; pralidoxime regenerates the enzyme if given early.

stem: A patient receives botulinum toxin injections in the masseter muscles for masseter hypertrophy. How does the toxin weaken the muscle?
choices: It blocks nicotinic receptors on the motor end plate
It inhibits acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft
It blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in the nerve
It cleaves SNARE proteins needed to release ACh

stem: True or false: Eccrine sweat glands receive sympathetic fibers that release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors.
ex: Sweat glands are the classic exception: sympathetic innervation with cholinergic (M3) transmission. That is why antimuscarinic drugs stop sweating and can cause overheating.

stem: An eye drop dilates the pupil but leaves near focusing intact. Which receptor action explains this?

M3 blockade of the iris sphincter, as with tropicamide
M3 stimulation of the iris sphincter, as with pilocarpine

stem: At the low doses in dental local anesthetic cartridges, which receptors does absorbed epinephrine mainly act on?

β1 and β2: faster heart rate, slight fall in diastolic pressure
