Giving several cartridges of lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine puts him at risk of:
choices: Severe hypotension from unopposed β2 vasodilation
A sharp rise in blood pressure with reflex bradycardia
No effect, because propranolol blocks all epinephrine actions
ex: With a nonselective β-blocker (propranolol, nadolol, timolol), epinephrine's α1 effect is unopposed: hypertension with reflex bradycardia. Aspirate, inject slowly, limit epinephrine (about two cartridges of 1:100,000) and recheck vital signs. Cardioselective β-blockers carry much less risk.
why: Propranolol blocks β2, so vasodilation is what is lost; hypotension after epinephrine follows an α1 blocker (epinephrine reversal).
Both of those β effects are blocked by a nonselective β-blocker.
Propranolol blocks β2 vasodilation and β1, so epinephrine's α1 vasoconstriction is unopposed and the baroreflex then slows the heart. Limit epinephrine (about 0.04 mg) and check vital signs.
Propranolol blocks only β receptors; α1 receptors still respond, and that is the danger.

likely.t: Epinephrine's receptors and its interaction with nonselective β-blockers

stem: A patient in anaphylaxis is wheezing and her blood pressure is falling. Which drug would raise the pressure but do nothing for the bronchospasm, because it lacks β2 activity?
ex: Norepinephrine: α1, α2 > β1, no β2; a vasopressor for shock. Epinephrine: β1, β2 and α (dose-dependent); the anaphylaxis drug.
why: Epinephrine acts on α and β receptors, including β2, which is why it is first-line in anaphylaxis.
A short-acting β2 agonist: it relieves bronchospasm but does little for shock.
A long-acting β2 agonist for maintenance; it bronchodilates.
A mixed-acting decongestant that releases NE and stimulates α and β receptors, including β2; it isn't an emergency drug.
It acts on α1, α2 and β1 but not β2, so it constricts vessels without relaxing bronchi; IM epinephrine treats both problems.

stem: A patient taking clonidine for hypertension wants to stop it because of her dry mouth. How does clonidine lower blood pressure, and what can happen if she stops suddenly?
choices: Central α2 stimulation cuts sympathetic outflow; abrupt stopping can cause rebound hypertension
Peripheral α1 blockade dilates arterioles; stopping it brings back first-dose orthostatic hypotension
β1 blockade slows the heart; stopping causes bronchospasm
Central α2 blockade raises NE release; stopping causes hypotension
ex: Clonidine: central α2 agonist for hypertension, ADHD and opioid withdrawal; side effects are dry mouth, sedation and rebound hypertension if stopped abruptly. Methyldopa is a prodrug of a central α2 agonist, used for hypertension in pregnancy.
why: Clonidine (and methyldopa) stimulate α2 receptors in the brainstem; sudden withdrawal releases a surge of norepinephrine. She should taper with her physician rather than stop.
That describes prazosin or terazosin; first-dose orthostatic hypotension belongs to α1 blockers.
That describes a β-blocker; clonidine has no β-blocking action.
Clonidine is an α2 agonist, not a blocker; α2 stimulation lowers NE release.

stem: Which statement about β-blockers is false?
choices: Metoprolol and atenolol are relatively β1-selective
Propranolol is β1-selective, so it is preferred in asthma
They can hide the fast pulse and tremor that warn a diabetic patient of hypoglycemia
Carvedilol blocks α1 as well as β receptors
ex: β1-selective (cardioselective): atenolol, metoprolol, betaxolol. Nonselective: propranolol, nadolol, timolol. α1 + β: carvedilol, labetalol. Watch for bronchospasm, bradycardia, fatigue and masked hypoglycemia.
why: This is true: oral drugs starting with A to M are mostly β1-selective, though selectivity fades at higher doses.
This is the false one: propranolol is nonselective (β1 and β2) and can trigger bronchospasm; metoprolol or atenolol are the relatively selective choices, still used with caution.
This is true: sweating remains, but the warning tachycardia and tremor are blunted, and recovery can be slower with nonselective drugs.
This is true: carvedilol and labetalol add α1 blockade (vasodilation), useful in heart failure and hypertension.

likely.t: α- and β-blockers and central α2 agonists

stem:
A 71-year-old man is finishing a long appointment.
History: benign prostatic hyperplasia, hypertension
Medications: terazosin (started last week), lisinopril
Vitals at the start: BP 128/78
What should you do before he leaves the chair?
choices: Avoid any epinephrine in his local anesthetic for the next week
Check for bronchospasm before he stands
Raise the chair slowly and let him sit before standing
ex: α1 blockers (-osin: prazosin, terazosin, tamsulosin) treat hypertension and BPH; tamsulosin is α1A-selective for the prostate. Their main side effect is orthostatic hypotension, worst after the first dose.
why: An α1 blocker doesn't make normal dental doses of epinephrine dangerous; nonselective β-blockers are the ones that call for epinephrine limits.
Bronchospasm is a risk of nonselective β-blockers, not α1 blockers.
α1 blockers relax vascular smooth muscle and cause orthostatic hypotension, worst in the first days of treatment; a slow return to upright prevents fainting.
α1 blockade causes a reflex fast heart rate if anything, not bradycardia.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Brimonidine lowers intraocular pressure by blocking α2 receptors in the eye.
2. Betaxolol eye drops are β1-selective and less likely than timolol to trigger bronchospasm.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Glaucoma drugs: brimonidine (α2 agonist), timolol (nonselective β-blocker), betaxolol (β1-selective), latanoprost (PGF2α analog), pilocarpine and carbachol (muscarinic agonists).
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: brimonidine is an α2 agonist: it lowers aqueous humor production and increases outflow.
Statement 2 is true, not false: timolol is nonselective and can be absorbed enough to cause bronchospasm or bradycardia; betaxolol is the safer drop in lung disease.

stem:
A 68-year-old woman starts oxybutynin for urge incontinence. Which effects of its muscarinic blockade should she expect?
1. Dry mouth that raises her caries risk
2. Constipation
3. Constricted pupils
4. A faster heart rate
ex: Antimuscarinic side effects are the reverse of DUMBBELSS: dry mouth and eyes, constipation, urinary retention, fast heart rate, dilated pupils with blurred near vision, less sweating, and confusion in older adults (the Beers list).
why: It leaves out 4, which is true: blocking M2 receptors at the SA node removes the vagal brake on the heart.

It includes 3, which is false: muscarinic blockade relaxes the iris sphincter, so the pupils dilate (and near focus blurs). It leaves out 4, which is true: blocking M2 receptors at the SA node removes the vagal brake on the heart.
Statements 1, 2 and 4 are true. Statement 3 is false: muscarinic blockade relaxes the iris sphincter, so the pupils dilate (and near focus blurs).

It includes 3, which is false: muscarinic blockade relaxes the iris sphincter, so the pupils dilate (and near focus blurs). It leaves out 1, which is true: blocking M3 receptors on the salivary glands reduces saliva; long-term use brings caries, candidiasis and periodontal problems.

likely.t: Muscarinic agonists and antagonists: uses and side effects

stem: True or false: Pyridostigmine treats Alzheimer disease because it crosses the blood-brain barrier easily.
ex: Pyridostigmine is a charged cholinesterase inhibitor that stays out of the brain and treats myasthenia gravis. Rivastigmine and donepezil treat Alzheimer disease; physostigmine enters the brain and reverses antimuscarinic delirium.
why: Pyridostigmine is a charged (quaternary) cholinesterase inhibitor that barely enters the brain; it treats myasthenia gravis, while rivastigmine and donepezil treat Alzheimer disease.
Pyridostigmine is for myasthenia gravis and stays out of the brain; physostigmine, rivastigmine and donepezil are the ones that enter it.

likely.t: Cholinesterase inhibitors and organophosphate poisoning

stem: Each of the following is an effect of M3 muscarinic stimulation EXCEPT:
ex: M3 (Gq): smooth muscle contraction (bronchi, gut, detrusor), sphincter relaxation, gland secretion, miosis and accommodation. M2 (Gi): slows the heart.
why: M3 receptors on the salivary glands drive watery secretion (pilocarpine).
M3 contracts the iris sphincter.
The parasympathetic signal to void (bethanechol treats urinary retention).
M3 stimulation constricts bronchial smooth muscle and increases secretions; bronchodilation comes from β2 stimulation or from M3 blockade (tiotropium).
M3 contracts gut smooth muscle and relaxes the sphincters.

stem: Which drug is matched with its correct use?
ex: Antimuscarinic uses: atropine (bradycardia, secretions, organophosphate poisoning), scopolamine (motion sickness), oxybutynin and darifenacin (overactive bladder), tiotropium (COPD), tropicamide (eye exams), hyoscyamine and dicyclomine (IBS).
why: Central muscarinic blockade in the vestibular pathway, from a patch behind the ear.
Tiotropium is an inhaled long-acting antimuscarinic for COPD; oxybutynin and darifenacin treat overactive bladder.
Bethanechol treats urinary retention and ileus; carbachol is used for surgical miosis.
Tamsulosin is an α1A blocker for BPH.

stem: Cocaine applied to the nasal mucosa both numbs and blanches it. Which actions explain this?
choices: Sodium channel block plus release of stored norepinephrine from vesicles
Na+ channel block plus norepinephrine reuptake block
Direct α1 stimulation plus MAO inhibition
ex: Indirect sympathomimetics: amphetamine releases NE and dopamine from vesicles; cocaine blocks NE, dopamine and serotonin reuptake; pseudoephedrine is mixed (releases NE and acts directly).
why: Releasing NE from vesicles is the amphetamine mechanism; cocaine blocks reuptake.
Like other local anesthetics it blocks sodium channels; blocking NE reuptake leaves more NE on α1 receptors, so vessels constrict. It is the only local anesthetic that does this.
Cocaine doesn't bind α1 directly or inhibit MAO; it raises NE by blocking its reuptake.
Neither explains numbness or vasoconstriction.

stem:
A 67-year-old man needs pain control after extraction of #19.
History: hypertension, chronic kidney disease (stage 3), atrial fibrillation
Medications: lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, warfarin
Which analgesic is the best first choice?
ex: Acetaminophen is the first choice for patients on anticoagulants or with kidney disease, ulcers, aspirin-sensitive asthma or pregnancy. NSAIDs with warfarin raise bleeding risk; NSAIDs with ACE inhibitors or ARBs and diuretics can cause acute kidney injury.
why: NSAIDs add bleeding risk with warfarin and, with an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic, can injure the kidneys and raise blood pressure.
No antiplatelet effect, no GI bleeding and no effect on kidney prostaglandins; keep within the daily limit, since regular high doses can nudge the INR up.
Less GI bleeding than other NSAIDs, but the same kidney and blood pressure effects and more cardiovascular risk.
The same NSAID problems as ibuprofen, lasting longer (half-life about 14 hours).
An irreversible antiplatelet effect on top of warfarin, plus GI bleeding.

likely.t: Aspirin, NSAIDs and COX-2 selectivity: harms and interactions

stem: Why does a single dose of aspirin impair platelet function for about a week, while ibuprofen's effect lasts only hours?
choices: Aspirin has a half-life of about 7 days
Aspirin blocks endothelial COX-2, the enzyme that makes platelet thromboxane
Ibuprofen is a prodrug that needs activation
Platelet COX-1 is acetylated for good, and platelets can't replace it
ex: Aspirin is the only irreversible COX inhibitor. Low-dose aspirin (81 mg) is an antiplatelet drug; its effect lasts the life of the platelet, 7–10 days.
why: Aspirin itself lasts only 15–20 minutes in plasma; the effect outlasts the drug.
Platelets make thromboxane A2 with COX-1; endothelial COX-2 makes prostacyclin.
Ibuprofen is active as given; it blocks COX reversibly, so platelets recover once it is cleared.
Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX; platelets have no nucleus to make new enzyme, so thromboxane A2 stays low for the platelet's 7–10-day life.

likely.t: Aspirin, NSAIDs and COX-2 selectivity: harms and interactions

stem:
A 22-year-old took about 15 g of acetaminophen over several hours for a toothache, about 6 hours ago.
Symptoms: nausea, sweating
Labs: liver enzymes starting to rise
Which treatment should be given?
ex: CYP2E1 turns a little acetaminophen into NAPQI, which glutathione normally neutralizes. An overdose (or chronic alcohol use, which induces CYP2E1 and depletes glutathione) lets NAPQI destroy hepatocytes. N-acetylcysteine restores glutathione.
why: An opioid antagonist; it does nothing for acetaminophen toxicity.
It reverses benzodiazepines.
It rescues normal cells from methotrexate.
It replenishes glutathione so NAPQI is neutralized; it protects the liver best within 8–10 hours of the overdose.
It alkalinizes the urine to clear salicylate (aspirin), not acetaminophen.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Acetaminophen reduces inflammation as well as ibuprofen because it blocks COX in peripheral tissues.

choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Acetaminophen acts centrally: analgesic and antipyretic, almost no anti-inflammatory or antiplatelet effect. Celecoxib spares COX-1, so it spares platelets too.
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: acetaminophen works mainly in the central nervous system; it relieves pain and fever but has almost no anti-inflammatory effect. Statement 2 is false, not true: platelets make thromboxane with COX-1, so a COX-2-selective drug has no antiplatelet effect; aspirin is the antiplatelet NSAID.

stem: True or false: Selective COX-2 inhibitors such as celecoxib cause fewer GI ulcers than nonselective NSAIDs but carry a higher risk of heart attack and stroke.
ex: Sparing COX-1 spares the stomach, but cutting endothelial prostacyclin (COX-2) while platelet thromboxane (COX-1) continues tips the balance toward clotting. Celecoxib is also a sulfonamide.
why: They spare COX-1's gastric protection, but cutting endothelial prostacyclin while platelet thromboxane continues tips the balance toward clotting.
Both parts hold: less GI toxicity, more cardiovascular risk.

stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis who needs a long-term NSAID is also prescribed misoprostol, a PGE1 analog. What is it for?
choices: Protecting the stomach from NSAID ulcers
Blocking platelet aggregation to prevent MI
ex: PGE: gastric protection, ductus patency, uterine contraction, erectile function (alprostadil). PGF2α: uterine contraction, lower intraocular pressure (latanoprost, bimatoprost), eyelash growth. PGI2: vasodilation, inhibits platelets. TXA2: platelet aggregation, vasoconstriction.
why: That is the PGF2α analogs, such as latanoprost.
PGE lowers gastric acid and increases mucus and bicarbonate, replacing what NSAIDs take away (it can cause diarrhea and is avoided in pregnancy).
Prostacyclin (PGI2) inhibits platelets; misoprostol is used for the stomach.
PGE keeps the ductus open (alprostadil); NSAIDs close it.

stem: Why do corticosteroids reduce both prostaglandins and leukotrienes, while NSAIDs reduce only prostaglandins?
choices: They inhibit both COX-1 and COX-2 irreversibly
They block 5-lipoxygenase as well as COX
They inhibit phospholipase A2, upstream of COX
They block prostaglandin receptors on target cells
ex: Membrane phospholipids → (phospholipase A2) → arachidonic acid → COX → prostaglandins, prostacyclin, thromboxane; or → lipoxygenase → leukotrienes. Shunting toward leukotrienes is why aspirin and NSAIDs can trigger asthma in sensitive patients.
why: That is aspirin's action, which leaves the leukotriene branch running.
Zileuton blocks 5-lipoxygenase; steroids act further upstream.
Phospholipase A2 frees arachidonic acid for both branches; NSAIDs act at COX, so the lipoxygenase branch (leukotrienes) keeps running.
Steroids cut the production of eicosanoids rather than blocking their receptors.

stem: Which pair of effects comes mainly from mu-opioid receptor activation?
choices: Tachycardia and a rise in blood pressure
ex: Mu: analgesia, euphoria, respiratory depression, miosis, constipation, dependence. Kappa: analgesia, sedation, dysphoria. Delta: analgesia (enkephalins). All are Gi-coupled.
why: Dysphoria is the kappa receptor's effect.
Those are signs of opioid withdrawal, the reverse of mu activation.
Opioids tend to cause bradycardia and hypotension.
Mu receptors mediate analgesia, euphoria, respiratory depression (a blunted response to CO2), miosis, constipation and dependence.

likely.t: Opioid receptor effects, tolerance, partial agonists and naloxone

stem: True or false: Patients on long-term opioids become tolerant to constipation and miosis, as they do to analgesia.
ex: Tolerance develops to analgesia, euphoria, sedation, nausea and respiratory depression, but not to constipation or miosis. Long-term users still have pinpoint pupils and need a bowel regimen.
why: Constipation and miosis persist with long-term use; that is why a bowel regimen (or a peripheral antagonist such as methylnaltrexone) is needed.
Tolerance doesn't develop to constipation or miosis, even though it does to analgesia, euphoria and respiratory depression.

likely.t: Opioid receptor effects, tolerance, partial agonists and naloxone

stem:
A 41-year-old woman needs pain relief after surgical extraction of an impacted molar.
History: depression; epilepsy, well controlled
Medications: sertraline, levetiracetam
Which analgesic should be avoided?
ex: Tramadol is a weak mu agonist (a prodrug activated by CYP2D6) that also inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake. Serotonin syndrome (agitation, fever, clonus, hyperreflexia) can follow its use with SSRIs or SNRIs; it also lowers the seizure threshold. Schedule IV.
why: Besides acting on mu receptors it blocks serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake: with sertraline it risks serotonin syndrome, and it lowers the seizure threshold.
A good choice here, alone or with acetaminophen; no serotonin or seizure concern.
Safe with sertraline and levetiracetam at normal doses.
No meaningful serotonin reuptake effect; usable for a short course if an opioid is needed.

stem:
A 34-year-old man has many new cervical caries.
History: opioid use disorder, in recovery for 2 years
Medications: buprenorphine-naloxone sublingual film daily
Which statement about his medication is accurate?
choices: A full mu agonist with no ceiling on respiratory depression
A partial mu agonist; dissolving it in the mouth is linked to caries
A pure mu antagonist, so no opioid will ever relieve his pain
The naloxone is well absorbed under the tongue and blocks the buprenorphine
ex: Buprenorphine: high-affinity partial mu agonist with a ceiling on respiratory depression; it can precipitate withdrawal in someone dependent on full agonists. Naloxone is added to deter injection.
why: That describes methadone or heroin; buprenorphine is a partial agonist with a ceiling effect.

Buprenorphine binds mu receptors tightly but activates them only partly (a ceiling on respiratory depression). Films and tablets dissolved in the mouth are linked to caries, so prevention and regular dental visits matter.
Naltrexone and naloxone are the pure antagonists; with buprenorphine, pain is managed with non-opioids first, together with his prescriber.
Naloxone is poorly absorbed sublingually; it is there to cause withdrawal if the film is dissolved and injected.

stem:
A 30-year-old found unresponsive is breathing 4 times a minute with pinpoint pupils. Intranasal naloxone wakes him within minutes. About an hour later he is drowsy and breathing slowly again.
What explains the relapse?
choices: Naloxone is a partial agonist that adds to the opioid
Naloxone wears off before the opioid does
He has become tolerant to naloxone
ex: Naloxone works within minutes (IV fastest; IM and intranasal a few minutes longer) and lasts 30–120 minutes, shorter than many opioids, so re-sedation is common. It can precipitate withdrawal in dependent patients.
why: Naloxone is a pure competitive antagonist with no agonist effect.
It worked, so it was absorbed; intranasal, IM and IV naloxone all reach the circulation (IV fastest).
Naloxone lasts about 30–120 minutes; methadone, fentanyl and extended-release opioids last longer, so watch the patient and redose.
Tolerance to naloxone's blockade doesn't develop in an hour; the opioid simply outlasted it.

stem:
A 25-year-old is brought in agitated after taking an unknown drug.
Temperature 39.4 °C, HR 132, BP 162/96
Pupils 7 mm; skin hot, flushed and dry; no bowel sounds; distended bladder
Which statements are true?
1. The dry skin points to an antimuscarinic rather than a sympathomimetic toxidrome.
2. Naloxone is the specific antidote.
3. Diphenhydramine or jimson weed could cause this picture.
4. Benzodiazepines are used to control the agitation.
ex: Hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter, full as a flask: the antimuscarinic toxidrome. Sympathomimetic poisoning looks similar but the skin is wet. Treat with benzodiazepines and cooling; physostigmine for a pure antimuscarinic poisoning.
why: It includes 2, which is false: naloxone reverses opioids; physostigmine is the antidote for a pure antimuscarinic poisoning. It leaves out 4, which is true: benzodiazepines treat agitation and seizures in both antimuscarinic and sympathomimetic poisoning.

It includes 2, which is false: naloxone reverses opioids; physostigmine is the antidote for a pure antimuscarinic poisoning. It leaves out 3, which is true: antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, scopolamine and plants such as jimson weed are common causes.
It leaves out 4, which is true: benzodiazepines treat agitation and seizures in both antimuscarinic and sympathomimetic poisoning.
Statements 1, 3 and 4 are true. Statement 2 is false: naloxone reverses opioids; physostigmine is the antidote for a pure antimuscarinic poisoning.

stem: A prescription reads: "Sig: 1 cap po q6h prn pain." What does it tell the patient?
choices: Take one capsule by mouth six times a day, every day, for the pain
Take one capsule after meals every 6 hours for pain
Take one capsule at bedtime and every 6 hours
Take one capsule by mouth every 6 hours as needed for pain
ex: Common abbreviations: po (by mouth), prn (as needed), q4h/q6h (every 4/6 hours), bid/tid/qid (2/3/4 times a day), hs (at bedtime), ac/pc (before/after meals), stat (now), disp (dispense), sig (directions).
why: Six times a day isn't q6h; q6h is every 6 hours (at most four doses a day), and prn means only when needed.
After meals is pc; po means by mouth.
At bedtime is hs; prn means as needed.
po = by mouth, q6h = every 6 hours, prn = as needed.

likely.t: Prescription writing and DEA schedules

stem: A dentist prescribes hydrocodone with acetaminophen after a surgical extraction. Which statement about this prescription is true?
choices: It is Schedule II, so it can't be refilled
It is Schedule III and may be refilled 5 times in 6 months
It is Schedule IV, like tramadol
The acetaminophen makes it a noncontrolled drug
ex: Schedule II (oxycodone, hydrocodone, morphine, fentanyl, methadone): no refills. Schedules III and IV: up to 5 refills within 6 months. Every controlled-drug prescription carries the prescriber's DEA number.
why: Since 2014 all hydrocodone combinations are Schedule II: no refills, and the prescriber's DEA number must appear.
That rule is for Schedules III and IV (acetaminophen with codeine is Schedule III).
Tramadol and benzodiazepines are Schedule IV; hydrocodone combinations moved up to II.
Combining an opioid with acetaminophen doesn't take it off the schedules.

stem: Each of the following is good practice when writing a prescription EXCEPT:
choices: Using a leading zero, as in 0.5 mg
Writing a specific quantity to dispense
Adding a trailing zero, as in 5.0 mg
Including the DEA number on an opioid prescription
ex: Always a leading zero, never a trailing zero; spell out units and micrograms; prefer generic names; write a specific quantity; avoid abbreviations that are easily confused.
why: A leading zero keeps 0.5 mg from being read as 5 mg.
A quantity (in numbers and words for controlled drugs) limits errors and misuse.
A trailing zero can be misread as 50 mg if the decimal point is missed; write 5 mg.
"U" can be read as 0 or 4, so it is written in full.
Required on every controlled-substance prescription.

stem: Which statement about opioid overdose and its treatment is true?
choices: Methadone wears off sooner than naloxone, so redosing is rarely needed
Naltrexone is the first drug to give for an acute overdose
Pinpoint pupils, slow breathing and stupor are the classic triad
Dilated pupils and diarrhea are signs of opioid overdose
ex: Opioid toxidrome: miosis, respiratory depression, CNS depression. Treat the airway and give naloxone, then watch for re-sedation. Withdrawal: mydriasis, yawning, tearing, runny nose, goosebumps, diarrhea.
why: Methadone's half-life is long and variable (often more than a day); naloxone lasts 30–120 minutes, so redosing is often needed.
Naloxone is; naltrexone is a long-acting antagonist that prevents relapse.
Miosis, respiratory depression and CNS depression; severe cases add bradycardia, hypotension and hypothermia.
Those are withdrawal signs, the reverse of intoxication.

stem:
A 27-year-old man arrives for an elective extraction.
History: says he used cocaine "last night"
Vitals: BP 168/102, HR 118
Exam: dilated pupils, sweating, restless
What is the best course?
choices: Proceed using lidocaine with 1:50,000 epinephrine for hemostasis
Proceed, giving propranolol first so the epinephrine cannot raise his heart rate
Postpone the procedure and avoid epinephrine for at least 24 hours
ex: Signs of recent stimulant use (high blood pressure, fast pulse, dilated pupils, sweating) mean elective care waits, and epinephrine-containing anesthetic is avoided for 24 hours after cocaine or methamphetamine.
why: More epinephrine on top of cocaine's NE excess is the dangerous combination.
A nonselective β-blocker leaves cocaine's α1 effects unopposed and can raise the pressure further.
Cocaine isn't an opioid; naloxone does nothing.
Cocaine blocks NE reuptake; adding epinephrine can cause a hypertensive crisis, arrhythmia or MI. Reschedule, and refer if the signs persist.

stem:
A 64-year-old man is scheduled for scaling and root planing.
History: mechanical aortic valve placed 3 years ago
Allergies: none
Medications: warfarin
What antibiotic prophylaxis, if any, does he need?
choices: Amoxicillin 2 g by mouth 30–60 minutes before the procedure
Amoxicillin 500 mg three times a day for 7 days after the procedure
Clindamycin 600 mg by mouth 30–60 minutes before
None, because a prosthetic valve doesn't call for prophylaxis
ex: AHA 2021: prophylaxis for a prosthetic valve or valve repair material, previous infective endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease (unrepaired cyanotic, repaired with prosthetic material in the first 6 months, or with a residual defect) and a heart transplant with valve disease, before procedures that manipulate the gingiva or periapical tissue or perforate the mucosa. Adults: amoxicillin 2 g (children 50 mg/kg) 30–60 minutes before.
why: A prosthetic valve is one of the highest-risk conditions, and scaling manipulates the gingiva. One 2 g dose of amoxicillin before the visit is the standard (AHA 2021).
Prophylaxis is a single dose before the procedure, not a course afterward.
Clindamycin is no longer recommended for prophylaxis (more C. difficile risk), and he isn't allergic to penicillin anyway.
A prosthetic valve, or prosthetic material used to repair one, is the first item on the AHA's list.

stem: The same patient now reports that penicillin once gave him throat swelling and hives within minutes. Which regimen fits?
choices: Cephalexin 2 g by mouth 30–60 minutes before
Azithromycin 500 mg by mouth 30–60 minutes before
Clindamycin 600 mg by mouth, 30–60 minutes before the extraction
ex: Penicillin allergy, AHA 2021: cephalexin 2 g (only without anaphylaxis, angioedema or hives), azithromycin or clarithromycin 500 mg, or doxycycline 100 mg. Unable to take by mouth: ampicillin 2 g or cefazolin or ceftriaxone 1 g IM or IV.
why: Cephalexin is an option for a penicillin allergy only when the reaction wasn't anaphylaxis, angioedema or hives.
With a history of anaphylaxis, angioedema or hives to penicillin, avoid cephalosporins; azithromycin or clarithromycin 500 mg, or doxycycline 100 mg, are the choices.
The AHA dropped clindamycin from the list in 2021 because of C. difficile risk.
An antihistamine doesn't prevent anaphylaxis; a penicillin isn't given after a reaction like his.

stem:
A 58-year-old woman took clindamycin for 10 days for a dental abscess.
Now: six or more watery stools a day for 3 days, cramping, temperature 38.2 °C
Medications: lisinopril
What is the most likely cause, and what is the treatment?
choices: A higher dose of clindamycin for a shorter course
Loperamide to slow the diarrhea while she finishes the course
C. difficile overgrowth; treat with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin
IV vancomycin, because oral vancomycin isn't absorbed
