stem:
Patient: 56-year-old woman
Chief complaint: dry mouth for years; eyes feel gritty
Findings: rampant cervical caries, fissured tongue, bilateral parotid swelling; anti-SS-A and anti-SS-B positive; a labial minor salivary gland biopsy shows focal lymphocytic infiltrates
Which complication must she be monitored for?
choices: Squamous cell carcinoma of the parotid duct
ex: Sjögren syndrome is lymphocytic destruction of the salivary and lacrimal glands, with anti-SS-A/SS-B antibodies. Its feared complication is B-cell (often MALT) lymphoma, so a persistently enlarging gland needs a workup. Dental care: fluoride, saliva substitutes, pilocarpine or cevimeline.
why: Squamous carcinoma isn't the recognized Sjögren risk.
Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common salivary tumor but isn't tied to Sjögren syndrome.
Osteonecrosis follows antiresorptive drugs or radiation, not Sjögren syndrome.
Chronic lymphocytic stimulation in Sjögren syndrome raises the risk of B-cell (MALT) lymphoma.
Sjögren syndrome doesn't raise endocarditis risk.

likely.t: Sjögren syndrome (the most dentally relevant), lupus antibodies, scleroderma in the mouth, Graves vs Hashimoto

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. A positive ANA is highly specific for systemic lupus erythematosus.
2. Hydralazine and procainamide can cause drug-induced lupus.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: ANA is sensitive (positive in nearly all lupus) but not specific; anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are the specific antibodies. Hydralazine, procainamide and isoniazid can cause drug-induced lupus with anti-histone antibodies, which settles when the drug stops.
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: ANA is sensitive but not specific; anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are the specific tests.
Statement 2 is true, not false: hydralazine and procainamide are the classic causes of drug-induced lupus.

Statement 1 is false, not true: ANA is sensitive but not specific; anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are the specific tests. Statement 2 is true, not false: hydralazine and procainamide are the classic causes of drug-induced lupus.

Statement 1 is false: ANA is sensitive but not specific; anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are the specific tests. Statement 2 is true: hydralazine and procainamide are the classic causes of drug-induced lupus.

stem:
Patient: 49-year-old woman
Chief complaint: can't open wide enough for impressions
Findings: tight, shiny skin of the face and fingers; fingers turn white in the cold; small mouth opening; radiographs show uniform widening of the PDL space around many teeth
What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) overproduces collagen: tight skin, Raynaud phenomenon, dysphagia, and in the mouth microstomia, limited opening, xerostomia, uniform PDL widening and resorption of the mandibular angle.
why: Lupus gives a malar rash and oral ulcers, not microstomia and PDL widening.
Microstomia, Raynaud and uniform PDL widening are scleroderma.
Sjögren syndrome dries the mouth but doesn't tighten skin or widen the PDL.
Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness, not skin fibrosis.
Paget disease enlarges bone and causes hypercementosis in older adults.

stem: Each of the following is a feature of Graves disease EXCEPT:
choices: Antibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor
Low TSH with high free T4
Hürthle cells with lymphoid germinal centers
ex: Graves disease is an IgG that stimulates the TSH receptor: hyperthyroidism (low TSH, high T4), a diffuse goiter and exophthalmos. Hürthle cells with germinal centers are the histology of Hashimoto thyroiditis, the common cause of hypothyroidism.
why: Stimulating TSH-receptor antibodies cause Graves disease.
Graves disease is hyperthyroid: TSH is suppressed and T4 is high.
Exophthalmos is a hallmark of Graves disease.
Graves disease gives a diffuse goiter.
Hürthle cells and germinal centers are Hashimoto thyroiditis.

stem:
Patient: 52-year-old man brought in confused
History: heavy alcohol use, poor diet
Findings: wide-based unsteady gait, nystagmus and weakness of eye movements
Before IV glucose is given, which vitamin should he receive?
ex: Confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia in an alcoholic are Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency. Glucose metabolism uses up the little thiamine left, so thiamine goes in first. Thiamine deficiency also causes dry (neuropathy) and wet (heart failure) beriberi.
why: Niacin deficiency is pellagra: dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia.
B6 deficiency causes neuropathy and cheilosis, often from isoniazid.
Wernicke encephalopathy is thiamine deficiency; give thiamine before glucose.
B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia with posterior-column signs, not acute Wernicke encephalopathy.
Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding.

likely.t: Nutrient function and deficiency: thiamine, vitamin C, folate vs B12, kwashiorkor edema

stem:
Patient: 74-year-old widower who lives on tea and toast
Chief complaint: swollen gums that bleed when he eats
Findings: purple, spongy interdental papillae; pinpoint bleeds around hair follicles; corkscrew hairs; a leg wound that won't heal
Which step in collagen synthesis is failing?
ex: Vitamin C is the cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases. Without hydroxylation, procollagen can't form a stable triple helix, so vessels and wounds are weak: scurvy, with swollen bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs and poor healing.
why: Vitamin C is needed to hydroxylate proline and lysine; without it the triple helix is unstable.
Glycosylation follows hydroxylation and doesn't need vitamin C.
Propeptide cleavage happens outside the cell and isn't vitamin C-dependent.
Lysyl oxidase needs copper, not vitamin C.
Translation of the collagen chains is intact in scurvy.

stem: True or false: Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia with neurologic signs such as loss of vibration sense.
ex: Folate and B12 deficiency both cause megaloblastic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils. Only B12 deficiency damages myelin (posterior and lateral columns: vibration and position sense, ataxia). Giving folate alone can mask the anemia of B12 deficiency while the nerve damage goes on.
why: Neurologic signs point to B12, not folate.
Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia without neurologic signs; the neurologic damage belongs to B12.

stem: A 2-year-old weaned onto a diet of starchy gruel has a swollen abdomen and legs, peeling skin, light-colored hair and an enlarged fatty liver. Which finding best distinguishes this from marasmus?
choices: Loss of over 60% of body weight
ex: Kwashiorkor is protein lack out of proportion to calories: low albumin brings generalized edema that can hide the weight loss, plus skin and hair changes and a fatty liver. Marasmus is total calorie starvation with severe wasting and no edema. Both bring vitamin deficiencies and infections.
why: Over 60% weight loss defines marasmus.
Severe muscle and fat wasting is the picture of marasmus.
Both forms bring multiple vitamin deficiencies.
Edema from hypoalbuminemia is the discriminator for kwashiorkor.
Both forms weaken immunity.

stem:
Patient: 15-year-old boy
Chief complaint: aching pain and swelling above the knee for 2 months
Findings: radiograph shows a destructive lesion in the distal femoral metaphysis with a "sunburst" pattern and a Codman triangle
What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary malignant bone tumor: teens, metaphysis around the knee, tumor cells making osteoid, a sunburst pattern and a Codman triangle where the periosteum lifts. It spreads to the lungs.
why: Ewing sarcoma favors the diaphysis and shows "onion-skin" layering.
A teen with a destructive distal femoral metaphyseal lesion, sunburst and Codman triangle has osteosarcoma.
Giant cell tumor is epiphyseal, lytic and in adults 20-40.
Osteochondroma is a benign cartilage-capped stalk, not a destructive lesion.
Chondrosarcoma affects adults over 50, usually in the pelvis or shoulder.

likely.t: Bone tumors by age and site: metastases first, osteosarcoma, osteoid osteoma, giant cell tumor, Ewing sarcoma

stem: A 19-year-old man has deep pain in his tibia that is worst at night and goes away within an hour of taking aspirin. A radiograph shows a 1-cm lucent nidus surrounded by thick sclerotic cortex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Osteoid osteoma is a small (under 2 cm) cortical tumor of young men whose cells make prostaglandin E2: night pain that NSAIDs relieve, and a lucent nidus in sclerotic bone. Osteoblastoma is larger, prefers the spine and isn't relieved by NSAIDs.
why: Osteoblastoma is over 2 cm, usually in the spine, and NSAIDs don't relieve it.
Enchondroma sits in the medulla of the small bones of the hands and feet.
Ewing sarcoma is a destructive diaphyseal tumor of children with systemic signs.
A bone abscess doesn't respond to aspirin in this way; TB is not the classic cause of a Brodie abscess.
Night pain relieved by NSAIDs with a small nidus in sclerotic cortex is osteoid osteoma (PGE2).

stem: Each of the following commonly metastasizes to bone EXCEPT:
choices: Basal cell carcinoma of the skin
ex: Most tumors found in bone are metastases, from breast, lung, thyroid, kidney and prostate ("BLT with a kosher pickle"). Basal cell carcinoma is locally destructive but almost never metastasizes.
why: Breast cancer is a leading source of bone metastases.
Prostate cancer sends classic blastic bone metastases.
Basal cell carcinoma almost never metastasizes.
Kidney (renal cell) cancer sends lytic bone metastases.
Lung cancer commonly spreads to bone.

stem:
Patient: 52-year-old woman
Chief complaint: painful mouth sores for 2 months; now blisters on her chest
Findings: ragged erosions of the buccal mucosa and gingiva; flaccid skin bullae that rupture easily; rubbing normal-looking skin makes the epidermis slide off
What does a biopsy most likely show?
choices: Suprabasal acantholysis from antibodies to desmoglein 3
A subepidermal split from antibodies to BP180
Granular IgA in the dermal papillae
A band of T lymphocytes destroying the basal cells
ex: Pemphigus vulgaris is IgG against desmoglein 3 (and 1) in desmosomes: keratinocytes come apart above the basal layer, leaving a "tombstone" row; immunofluorescence is net-like between cells. Oral lesions usually appear first, bullae are flaccid and the Nikolsky sign is positive.
why: Oral lesions first, flaccid bullae and a positive Nikolsky sign mean pemphigus: anti-desmoglein 3 and suprabasal acantholysis.
A subepidermal split from anti-BP180 is pemphigoid, with tense bullae and a negative Nikolsky sign.
Granular IgA in the papillae is dermatitis herpetiformis.
A lichenoid band of T cells is lichen planus.
Spongiosis is the pattern of eczema.

likely.t: Pemphigus vs pemphigoid (desmosome vs hemidesmosome, intra- vs subepidermal, Nikolsky), dermatitis herpetiformis and lichen planus

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Bullous pemphigoid targets hemidesmosome proteins, so its blisters are subepidermal and tense.
2. The Nikolsky sign is typically positive in bullous pemphigoid.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Pemphigoid antibodies bind BP180 and BP230 in the hemidesmosomes, so the whole epidermis lifts off the basement membrane as a tense, durable bulla. Because the epidermis itself stays intact, the Nikolsky sign is negative; a positive sign points to pemphigus.
why: Statement 2 is false, not true: the Nikolsky sign is negative in pemphigoid; it is positive in pemphigus.
Statement 1 is true, not false: anti-BP180 and BP230 split the epidermis from the basement membrane, giving tense bullae.

Statement 1 is true: anti-BP180 and BP230 split the epidermis from the basement membrane, giving tense bullae. Statement 2 is false: the Nikolsky sign is negative in pemphigoid; it is positive in pemphigus.

Statement 1 is true, not false: anti-BP180 and BP230 split the epidermis from the basement membrane, giving tense bullae. Statement 2 is false, not true: the Nikolsky sign is negative in pemphigoid; it is positive in pemphigus.

likely.t: Pemphigus vs pemphigoid (desmosome vs hemidesmosome, intra- vs subepidermal, Nikolsky), dermatitis herpetiformis and lichen planus

stem: A 30-year-old man has intensely itchy, grouped vesicles on his elbows, knees and buttocks. Biopsy shows granular IgA deposits in the dermal papillae. Which condition is he most likely to have as well?
ex: Dermatitis herpetiformis is IgA against epidermal transglutaminase, the skin form of gluten sensitivity: nearly every patient has celiac disease, often without gut symptoms. It responds to dapsone and a gluten-free diet.
why: Crohn disease brings other skin signs, such as erythema nodosum.
Lupus gives a malar rash and granular IgG/C3 at the junction, not papillary IgA.
Hepatitis C is linked to lichen planus.
Dermatitis herpetiformis is the skin form of celiac disease.
Myasthenia gravis is linked to thymoma, not this rash.

stem:
Patient: 55-year-old woman
Chief complaint: her cheeks sting with spicy food
Findings: lacy white lines on both buccal mucosae that don't rub off, with a few red erosions; purple, flat-topped itchy papules on her wrists
Which histologic finding best fits?
choices: Intraepithelial clefts above the basal row
A band of T lymphocytes along the basal layer
ex: Bilateral lacy white striae (reticular) and erosions with purple polygonal skin papules are lichen planus: cytotoxic T cells form a band at the epithelial-connective tissue junction and destroy basal cells, leaving sawtooth rete ridges and Civatte bodies. Topical steroids are the treatment.
why: Suprabasal clefts are pemphigus.
Lichen planus is a band-like T-cell infiltrate destroying the basal layer.
A subepithelial split is pemphigoid.
Parakeratosis with Munro microabscesses is psoriasis.
Hyphae would mean candidiasis, which wipes off.

stem:
Patient: 68-year-old retired farmer
Chief complaint: a sore on his upper lip that bleeds and heals over and over
Findings: 8-mm pearly papule with rolled borders, central crust and telangiectasias; no enlarged nodes
What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer: a pearly papule with rolled borders and telangiectasias on the sun-exposed face, the upper lip more than the lower. It is locally destructive (the "rodent ulcer") but almost never metastasizes.
why: SCC is usually a scaly, keratotic ulcer and favors the lower lip.
Nodular melanoma is usually dark and grows fast.
Actinic keratosis is a rough scaly patch, not a pearly papule.
Seborrheic keratosis is a waxy "stuck-on" plaque.
A pearly, rolled-border, telangiectatic papule on the upper lip is basal cell carcinoma.

likely.t: Basal cell vs squamous cell carcinoma vs melanoma (ABCDE, Breslow thickness)

stem: True or false: In melanoma, the depth of invasion (Breslow thickness) is the strongest predictor of prognosis.
ex: Breslow thickness, measured in millimeters from the granular layer to the deepest tumor cell, is the strongest predictor of metastasis and survival. ABCDE (asymmetry, border, color, diameter over 6 mm, evolving) is for spotting a suspicious lesion.
why: Breslow thickness is melanoma's most important prognostic factor.
The statement is true: deeper melanomas metastasize more, so Breslow thickness predicts prognosis best.

likely.t: Basal cell vs squamous cell carcinoma vs melanoma (ABCDE, Breslow thickness)

stem: Which statement about the cells of the epidermis is FALSE?
choices: Langerhans cells are antigen-presenting cells with Birbeck granules
Merkel cells in the basal layer help sense light touch
Darker skin has more melanocytes per area
Keratinocytes of the stratum spinosum are joined by desmosomes
ex: People of every skin color have about the same number of melanocytes; darker skin has more, larger and more widely spread melanosomes. The other statements are true.
why: Langerhans cells are the epidermis's antigen-presenting cells, with Birbeck granules.
Merkel cells sit in the basal layer and work with nerve endings in touch.
Melanocyte numbers are similar in all skin colors; melanosome size, number and spread differ.
Desmosomes give the stratum spinosum its "spiny" look.

stem: A receptor in the dermal papillae of the fingertips responds to light touch and adapts quickly. Which receptor is it?
ex: Meissner corpuscles sit in the dermal papillae of hairless skin and detect light, discriminative touch, adapting quickly. Pacinian corpuscles are large, onion-layered and deep in the dermis and hypodermis, and detect vibration and deep pressure.
why: Superficial, in the dermal papillae, for light touch: Meissner.
Pacinian corpuscles lie deep and sense vibration.
Ruffini endings sense skin stretch and adapt slowly.
Free nerve endings carry pain and temperature.
Muscle spindles sense muscle stretch, not touch.

stem: True or false: Isotretinoin commonly causes cheilitis and dry mouth.
ex: Isotretinoin shrinks sebaceous glands and dries mucous membranes: cheilitis is nearly universal, and xerostomia, dry eyes and dry skin are common. It is a potent teratogen (the iPLEDGE program) and can raise triglycerides.
why: Cheilitis and xerostomia are the dental hallmarks of isotretinoin.
The statement is true: isotretinoin dries the lips and mouth in most patients.

likely.t: Dermatologic drugs: absorption, steroids vs calcineurin inhibitors, isotretinoin, permethrin, antifungals

stem: Each of the following increases how much of a topical drug is absorbed EXCEPT:
choices: Covering it with an occlusive dressing
Applying it to inflamed, broken skin
Applying it to the palms and soles
ex: The stratum corneum is the barrier, so absorption rises where it is thin (eyelids, face, scrotum), damaged or hydrated (occlusion), and in infants, who have more surface area per kilogram. The thick corneum of the palms and soles absorbs least.
why: Occlusion hydrates the stratum corneum and raises absorption.
Inflamed or broken skin has a weaker barrier.
Infants have more surface area per kilogram and a thinner barrier.
Palms and soles have the thickest stratum corneum, so they absorb least.
Eyelid skin is among the thinnest and absorbs readily.

stem: A 9-year-old has intensely itchy papules and thin burrows in the finger webs and wrists, worse at night; his brother itches too. Which topical drug is first-line?
ex: Burrows in the finger webs with night itching and affected contacts are scabies. Permethrin keeps the mite's nerve sodium channels open, paralyzing it; it also treats lice. Household contacts are treated at the same time.
why: Mupirocin is an antibacterial for impetigo.
Permethrin treats scabies (and lice).
Terbinafine is an antifungal (squalene epoxidase).
Ketoconazole is an azole antifungal.
Acyclovir treats herpesviruses.

stem: In the cross-bridge cycle, which event requires ATP to bind myosin?
ex: ATP binding releases the myosin head from actin; hydrolysis then re-cocks it, and release of Pi drives the power stroke. Without ATP, myosin stays bound (rigor mortis). Relaxation also needs ATP, for SERCA to pump calcium back into the SR.
why: Calcium binds troponin C without ATP.
The power stroke is driven by release of Pi and ADP, not ATP binding.
RyR1 opens through its link to the DHP receptor, not by ATP binding.
The nicotinic receptor is opened by ACh.
ATP binding is what lets myosin let go of actin; no ATP means rigor.

likely.t: Excitation-contraction coupling, troponin C, ATP in the cross-bridge cycle, sarcomere bands

stem:
During a skeletal muscle contraction, which statements about the sarcomere are true?
1. The A band shortens
2. The I band shortens
3. The H zone shortens
4. The Z lines move closer together
ex: Filaments slide; they don't shorten. The A band is the length of the thick filaments, so it stays the same. The I band (thin filaments only) and the H zone (thick only) shrink as the filaments overlap more, and the Z lines are pulled together.
why: It includes 1, which is false: the A band is the thick filament's length and doesn't change. It leaves out 4, which is true: the Z lines are pulled toward the M line.
It includes 1, which is false: the A band is the thick filament's length and doesn't change. It leaves out 2, which is true: the I band shrinks as the thin filaments slide in.
It leaves out 4, which is true: the Z lines are pulled toward the M line.
Statements 2, 3 and 4 are true. Statement 1 is false: the A band is the thick filament's length and doesn't change.

stem:
Patient: 19-year-old woman under general anesthesia for third molar extraction
History: given succinylcholine and sevoflurane
Findings: jaw rigidity right after induction, then rising end-tidal CO2, tachycardia and a temperature climbing past 39°C
What is the mechanism of the drug that treats this?
choices: It agonizes GABA-B receptors in the cord
It blocks calcium release through RyR1
ex: Masseter rigidity, hypercarbia, tachycardia and hyperthermia after succinylcholine or a volatile anesthetic are malignant hyperthermia: a RyR1 mutation releases calcium uncontrollably. Dantrolene blocks RyR1. Stop the trigger, cool the patient and treat hyperkalemia.
why: Cholinesterase inhibition (neostigmine) reverses nondepolarizing blockers.
GABA-B agonism is baclofen, for spasticity.
Dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia by blocking RyR1.
Encapsulation is sugammadex, which binds rocuronium and vecuronium.
Competitive nicotinic blockade is how rocuronium works.

likely.t: Succinylcholine (pseudocholinesterase, malignant hyperthermia), reversal with neostigmine or sugammadex, spasmolytics

stem: After a 10-minute procedure with succinylcholine, a patient is still apneic 3 hours later. His mother had the same problem after surgery. What best explains this?
ex: Succinylcholine is broken down by plasma pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase). An inherited atypical enzyme leaves the drug active for hours, so the patient needs ventilation until it wears off. A dibucaine test identifies the variant.
why: Inherited atypical pseudocholinesterase prolongs succinylcholine for hours.
RyR1 mutations cause malignant hyperthermia, not prolonged apnea.
ACh receptor antibodies are myasthenia gravis.
Hofmann elimination is spontaneous and is how cisatracurium is cleared, not succinylcholine.
Hyperkalemia is a risk of succinylcholine but doesn't prolong apnea.

stem: Which statement about reversing neuromuscular blockade is true?
choices: Neostigmine reverses a phase I succinylcholine block
Glycopyrrolate is added to block neostigmine's nicotinic effects
Sugammadex reverses rocuronium by encapsulating it
ex: Sugammadex binds rocuronium and vecuronium in solution. Neostigmine reverses nondepolarizing blockers but deepens a phase I succinylcholine block; glycopyrrolate (or atropine) is given with it to block muscarinic effects (bradycardia, secretions). Cisatracurium breaks down by Hofmann elimination, independent of the liver and kidneys.
why: Neostigmine deepens a phase I depolarizing block.
Glycopyrrolate blocks muscarinic effects; the nicotinic effect is the one wanted.
Cisatracurium undergoes Hofmann elimination, so organ failure barely changes it.
Sugammadex encapsulates rocuronium and vecuronium.

stem: Which muscle of mastication helps open the mouth and protrudes the mandible?
ex: The masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid elevate (close) the mandible. The lateral pterygoid pulls the condyle and disc forward, protruding the jaw and starting opening; acting on one side, it swings the jaw to the other.
why: The medial pterygoid closes the jaw.
The lateral pterygoid is the muscle of mastication that opens and protrudes.
The masseter closes the jaw.
The temporalis closes and retrudes the jaw.
The buccinator is a muscle of facial expression, not mastication.

stem: A patient with spasticity from multiple sclerosis takes a drug that activates GABA-B receptors in the spinal cord. Which drug is it?
ex: Baclofen is a GABA-B agonist that reduces spinal reflex activity in spasticity. Tizanidine is a central α2 agonist; diazepam enhances GABA-A; dantrolene acts in the muscle at RyR1; cyclobenzaprine, a tricyclic-like drug, is for acute muscle spasm, not spasticity.
why: Tizanidine is a central α2 agonist.
Dantrolene blocks RyR1 in the muscle itself.
Diazepam acts on GABA-A receptors.
Cyclobenzaprine treats acute local spasm and works like a tricyclic.
Baclofen is the GABA-B agonist.

stem: A general dentist declines to accept a new patient after learning from the medical history that the patient is HIV positive, though the patient needs only routine restorations. Which principle of the ADA Code does this violate?
ex: Section 4, justice (fairness): 4.A Patient selection. A dentist refers a patient with HIV only when another practitioner's skills or equipment are needed, as for any patient.
why: Autonomy (Section 1) covers self-determination and confidentiality; refusing care unfairly is a justice issue.
Beneficence (Section 3) is the duty to do good; the Code places patient selection under justice.
Veracity (Section 5) is about honesty in claims, fees and records.
Code 4.A forbids refusing patients because of disability, which includes HIV; advisory opinion 4.A.1 says to treat them on the same basis as others.
Nonmaleficence (Section 2) concerns avoiding harm; patient selection is under justice.

likely.t: The five principles in Code order and naming the principle a scenario turns on

stem:
Patient: 45-year-old man
Situation: has moved across town and owes a balance of $600
Request: his new dentist asks for his radiographs and a summary of his chart
What does the ADA Code require of his former dentist?
choices: Send the records only after the $600 balance has been paid in full, since the records belong to the practice
Send the original radiographs and keep no copy of them in the office
Send copies of the records and radiographs, free or for a nominal fee, though the balance is unpaid
Refuse the request, because records may be released only to the patient himself
ex: Code 1.B (patient autonomy): records are confidential, and the information that will help future treatment goes to the patient or the new dentist on request, free or at nominal cost, paid or not.
why: The obligation exists whether or not the account is paid; collect the debt separately.
The dentist keeps the originals and sends copies or summaries.
Advisory opinion 1.B.1: copies go to the patient or the new dentist whether or not the account is paid in full.
Code 1.B says to provide the information on request of the patient or another dental practitioner.

likely.t: Records, abandonment, emergencies, abuse reporting, postexposure duties and patients with HIV or hepatitis

stem: True or false: Under the ADA Code, a dentist may hold a patient's radiographs until the patient's account is paid in full.
ex: Advisory opinion 1.B.1: the obligation to furnish copies of records, including radiographs, exists whether or not the patient's account is paid in full.
why: Advisory opinion 1.B.1 says copies go to the patient or the new dentist whether or not the account is paid.
Holding records hostage to a bill is unethical; the debt is collected separately.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Recommending removal of sound amalgam restorations from a non-allergic patient to rid the body of toxins is unethical under the principle of veracity.
2. Under the ADA Code, recommending removal of any sound restorative material, not only amalgam, to rid the body of toxins is unethical.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: The Code's advisory opinion on amalgam (veracity): removing amalgam from a non-allergic patient for the alleged purpose of removing toxins, when done solely at the dentist's recommendation, is improper and unethical, and the same applies to any restorative material.
why: Statement 1 is true: the Code's advisory opinion on amalgam calls it improper and unethical when done at the dentist's recommendation. Statement 2 is true: the same advisory opinion applies the principle of veracity to recommending the removal of any restorative material.

Statement 1 is true, not false: the Code's advisory opinion on amalgam calls it improper and unethical when done at the dentist's recommendation. Statement 2 is true, not false: the same advisory opinion applies the principle of veracity to recommending the removal of any restorative material.
Statement 2 is true, not false: the same advisory opinion applies the principle of veracity to recommending the removal of any restorative material.
Statement 1 is true, not false: the Code's advisory opinion on amalgam calls it improper and unethical when done at the dentist's recommendation.

likely.t: Veracity and fees: amalgam removal, copayment waivers and overbilling, split fees, advertising and product sales

stem: Over several weeks, a dentist notices the smell of alcohol on her associate in the mornings and sees his hands shake during procedures. She has seen him treat patients this way. What does the ADA Code ask of her?
choices: Urge him to seek treatment, and report it to the dental society's professional assistance committee
Say nothing for now, and act only if one of his patients is actually harmed during a procedure
Tell each of his patients that he has been drinking before work, so they can choose another dentist
Call the police and have him removed from the office at once
ex: Code 2.D Personal impairment (nonmaleficence): practicing impaired is unethical; colleagues urge treatment and, with first-hand knowledge, report to the professional assistance committee.
why: Code 2.D: urge impaired colleagues to get treatment, and with first-hand knowledge that one is practicing impaired, report it to the professional assistance committee.
Waiting for harm fails the duty to protect patients (nonmaleficence).
Telling patients doesn't get him help or protect future patients; the Code routes this to the dental society.
The Code points to the dental society's assistance committee, not the police.

likely.t: Colleagues: justifiable criticism of prior work and the impaired colleague

stem:
Patient: 60-year-old woman
Treatment: midway through a three-unit bridge; the abutments are prepared and in temporaries
Issue: she has missed four appointments, and the dentist wants to end the relationship
What is the ethical way to do it?
choices: Dismiss her today by letter and remove her from the schedule
Give her adequate notice and time to find another dentist, without leaving her oral health at risk
Keep her as a patient and finish the bridge, because a dentist may never dismiss a patient once treatment has begun
Finish the bridge free of charge, then dismiss her
ex: Code 2.F Patient abandonment (nonmaleficence). In practice: a letter giving a reasonable period, emergency care available meanwhile, and records sent to the next dentist.
why: Ending treatment midcourse without adequate notice is patient abandonment.
Code 2.F: don't discontinue treatment without adequate notice and the chance to obtain another dentist, and don't jeopardize her oral health.
Dentists may end a relationship; they must do it without abandoning the patient.
Nothing requires free care; the duty is adequate notice and continuity of care.

stem: On a Saturday, a man who has never been your patient calls with facial swelling and severe pain from a lower molar. His own dentist is out of town. What does the Code require?
choices: Nothing, because he is not a patient of record
Treat the infection yourself, then keep him on as your own patient for all of his future dental care
Tell him to see his own dentist when the dentist returns next week
Make reasonable arrangements for his emergency care, then return him to his regular dentist
ex: Code 4.B Emergency service (justice): reasonable arrangements for patients of record and for others who call in an emergency.
why: 4.B extends the duty to patients not of record who contact you in an emergency.
After the emergency, return him to his regular dentist unless he says he prefers otherwise.
Waiting a week with spreading swelling isn't a reasonable arrangement for emergency care.
Code 4.B: dentists consulted in an emergency by patients not of record make reasonable arrangements for emergency care, then return them to their regular dentist.

stem:
Patient: 50-year-old man, new to your practice
Findings: three crowns placed two years ago by another dentist have open margins with recurrent caries
He asks, "Did my last dentist do a bad job?"
What is the most appropriate response?
choices: Tell him the previous dentist was negligent and that he should think about suing
Say nothing about the crowns, so as not to criticize a fellow dentist in front of a patient
Describe his current condition and needs without disparaging the earlier work
Report the previous dentist to the reviewing agency today, on the basis of this one case
ex: Code 4.C Justifiable criticism (justice): truthful, informed, justifiable comments; a difference of opinion isn't mistreatment; report gross or continual faulty treatment to the agency the dental society designates.
why: Unjustified disparaging comments violate 4.C and can be grounds for discipline.
Patients must be told their present oral health status.
Code 4.C and 4.C.1: inform patients of their present status without disparaging prior services, and where possible consult the previous dentist about the conditions under which the work was done.
The reporting duty is for gross or continual faulty treatment; a single case with an unknown history isn't that.

likely.t: Colleagues: justifiable criticism of prior work and the impaired colleague

stem: A dentist tells a patient he will accept her insurance payment as payment in full and won't collect her 20% copayment. He bills the insurer his full fee and doesn't tell it that the copayment is waived. This is:
choices: Acceptable, because waiving the copayment helps the patient afford her care
A breach of justice under the Code's rules on patient selection
Fee splitting with the insurance company
ex: Section 5, veracity, 5.B Representation of fees: the essence of overbilling is deception and misrepresentation to the third party.
why: Advisory opinion 5.B.1: waiving the copayment without telling the third party makes the charge look higher than it is.
A kind motive doesn't change the deception toward the insurer.
Patient selection (4.A) is about refusing patients unfairly.
Fee splitting is sharing collected fees with another party, for example for marketing (4.E).

likely.t: Veracity and fees: amalgam removal, copayment waivers and overbilling, split fees, advertising and product sales

stem: A dentist signs up with a social-coupon website. The site sells a $99 exam-and-cleaning coupon, keeps 50% of each sale, and sends the rest to the dentist. Under the ADA Code, this arrangement:
choices: Is ordinary advertising and therefore always allowed
Is fee splitting, which the Code forbids
Is allowed as long as the coupon's claims are truthful
Is allowed if each patient signs a consent form first
ex: Code 4.E Rebates and split fees (justice): the ban applies to any third party, including marketers, coupon sites and influencers paid a share of fees.
why: Paying for advertising is fine; paying with a share of each patient's fee is fee splitting.
Advisory opinion 4.E.1 names social coupons whose issuer keeps a defined share of the fee as fee splitting.
Truthful ads still can't be paid for with a percentage of the fees collected.
Patient consent doesn't make a split fee ethical.

stem:
Which of these actions are consistent with the ADA Code?
1. A practice keeps a retired dentist's name on its sign for three years, with no notice to the public.
2. A general dentist advertises implant services and states that they are provided by a general dentist.
3. A dentist who suspects a serious adverse reaction to a drug reports it to the FDA.
4. A dentist who sells an electric toothbrush in her office tells patients that she earns a commission on it.
ex: Name of practice (5.G): up to one year, longer only with prominent notice. General dentists announcing services (5.I) say they are general dentists. Serious adverse reactions go to the FDA, and product sales require disclosing financial incentives (5.D).
why: It includes 1, which is false: a departing dentist's name may stay for up to one year (5.G), and longer only with prominent public notice. It leaves out 4, which is true: Code 5.D asks dentists who sell products to disclose financial incentives that wouldn't be evident to the patient.
It leaves out 4, which is true: Code 5.D asks dentists who sell products to disclose financial incentives that wouldn't be evident to the patient.
Statements 2, 3 and 4 are true. Statement 1 is false: a departing dentist's name may stay for up to one year (5.G), and longer only with prominent public notice.
It leaves out 2, which is true: 5.I allows announcing services if the dentist says they are a general dentist.

stem: Which statement about how the ADA Code is structured is true?
choices: The Principles of Ethics are binding rules, while the Code of Professional Conduct is aspirational
A dentist's ethical duties under the Code never go beyond what the law requires
The Code of Professional Conduct is binding on ADA members, and violating it can lead to discipline
The advisory opinions are the five principles that form the Code's foundation
ex: Principles of Ethics: aspirational. Code of Professional Conduct: binding on members, adopted by the House of Delegates. Advisory opinions: the Council on Ethics, Bylaws and Judicial Affairs' interpretations.
why: It's the reverse: the principles are aspirational goals, and the Code of Professional Conduct is binding.
The Code says ethical obligations may, and often do, exceed legal duties.
Members agree to it as a condition of membership; censure, suspension or expulsion can follow a violation.
Advisory opinions are the Council's interpretations of the Code in specific situations; the five principles are a separate part.

likely.t: The five principles in Code order and naming the principle a scenario turns on

stem: True or false: A dentist who is the source of a patient's needlestick exposure has an ethical duty to share his own bloodborne pathogen status with the practitioner evaluating the patient and to be tested.
ex: Code 2.E (nonmaleficence): tell the exposed patient at once of the need for postexposure evaluation, refer them, and, as the source, share your status with the evaluating practitioner and submit to testing.
why: Code 2.E: inform the patient, refer for postexposure care, and, as the source, share status and submit to testing.
The Code states this duty outright, whatever the dentist's own status.

stem: A patient with hepatitis C needs scaling and root planing. Which statement about the ethics of his care is false?
choices: Decisions about his treatment should be made on the same basis as for any other patient
Referral is appropriate if another practitioner's skills, knowledge or equipment are needed
The dentist may consult his physician about whether treatment would seriously compromise his health
A dentist may decline to treat him because standard precautions can't protect the staff from hepatitis C
ex: Advisory opinion 4.A.1 (justice): patients with HIV, HBV, HCV or a disability are treated on the same basis as others.
why: This is true: advisory opinion 4.A.1.
This is true: 4.A.1 points to consultation and referral under 2.B.
This is true: 4.A.1 allows consulting the physician when appropriate.
This is the false one: standard precautions are designed for every patient, and advisory opinion 4.A.1 says treatment decisions are made on the same basis as for other patients.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Dentists must report suspected child abuse and neglect to the proper authorities as state law requires.
2. When an adult patient asks that suspected abuse not be reported and no law requires a report, the dentist should report it anyway.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Code 3.E (beneficence) requires knowing the signs and reporting suspected cases consistent with state law. Its advisory opinion adds that a competent adult's wish not to report is respected when no report is mandated, and other help is sought with permission.
why: Statement 2 is false, not true: the advisory opinion under 3.E asks the dentist to respect a competent adult's wishes when a report isn't mandated, and to seek other help with permission.
Statement 1 is true, not false: Code 3.E obliges dentists to know the signs and report suspected cases consistent with state law.

Statement 1 is true: Code 3.E obliges dentists to know the signs and report suspected cases consistent with state law. Statement 2 is false: the advisory opinion under 3.E asks the dentist to respect a competent adult's wishes when a report isn't mandated, and to seek other help with permission.

Statement 1 is true, not false: Code 3.E obliges dentists to know the signs and report suspected cases consistent with state law. Statement 2 is false, not true: the advisory opinion under 3.E asks the dentist to respect a competent adult's wishes when a report isn't mandated, and to seek other help with permission.

stem: Each of the following is unethical under the veracity section of the ADA Code EXCEPT:
choices: Advertising the practice's services in ads that are not false or misleading
Charging a patient a higher fee because she has dental insurance
Reporting a later treatment date so that the patient's plan will cover the work
Recommending treatment that the patient doesn't need
ex: Veracity covers representation of care and fees, conflicts of interest, devices, advertising and announcements. Truthful advertising is ethical.
why: Advertising is allowed (5.F); only advertising that is false or misleading in a material respect is unethical.
Advisory opinion 5.B.2 calls this overbilling.
Advisory opinion 5.B.4: a false representation to the third party.
Advisory opinion 5.B.6: recommending unnecessary services is unethical.

stem: Before preparing a crown, a dentist explains the procedure, its risks and costs, and the alternatives (an onlay, a large filling, or no treatment), then lets the patient decide. Which principle does this chiefly honor?
ex: Section 1, patient autonomy (self-governance): 1.A Patient involvement is the Code's basis for informed consent.
why: Beneficence is promoting the patient's welfare; informing the patient and letting them choose is autonomy.
Code 1.A: inform the patient of the proposed treatment and reasonable alternatives so they can take part in the decision.
Justice is fairness in dealings with patients, colleagues and society.
Nonmaleficence is the duty to avoid harm.

stem: True or false: A dentist who sells a whitening product in her office may rely on the manufacturer's safety claims and need not mention that she earns a commission on it.
ex: Advisory opinion 5.D.2 (veracity): for a health-related product the dentist has an independent duty to check that the claims rest on accepted science, and must disclose financial incentives that wouldn't be evident to the patient.
why: Advisory opinion 5.D.2 says she has an independent duty to verify health claims and must disclose financial incentives the patient wouldn't see.
Both halves are wrong: she must check the claims herself and disclose the commission.

stem:
Patient: 52-year-old man
Plan: extract #30 and place an implant
The dentist explains the procedure, its benefits, its risks (nerve injury, infection, implant failure) and its cost, and the patient signs the consent form.
He was never told about a bridge, a removable partial denture, or leaving the space.
Which element of informed consent is missing?
choices: The material risks of the proposed procedure
The patient's signature on the consent form
The cost of the proposed treatment plan
The reasonable alternatives, including no treatment
ex: Disclose the diagnosis, the proposed treatment, its benefits and risks, the alternatives (including no treatment) and their risks, and the costs; then let the patient with capacity choose freely.
why: Nerve injury, infection and failure were explained.
He signed; a signature documents consent but doesn't replace the discussion.
The cost was explained.
Consent requires the alternatives and their risks, including doing nothing (Code 1.A: "any reasonable alternatives").

likely.t: Informed consent and refusal: what to disclose, Canterbury's reasonable-patient standard, capacity and consent for minors

stem: Canterbury v. Spence (1972) set which standard for what a clinician must disclose before treatment?
choices: Risks a reasonable person in the patient's position would find significant
Whatever other physicians in the same community customarily tell their patients
Every possible risk of the procedure, however rare or minor it may be
Whatever the treating clinician judges is best for this patient to hear
ex: Schloendorff (1914): the right to decide about one's own body. Salgo (1957): first use of "informed consent." Canterbury (1972): the reasonable-patient standard.
why: The court tied disclosure to the patient's right to decide: a risk is material if a reasonable person in that position would attach significance to it.
That is the older professional standard that Canterbury moved away from.
The court said full disclosure of every risk isn't required; material risks are.
That is medical paternalism; the case grounded the duty in the patient's autonomy.

likely.t: Informed consent and refusal: what to disclose, Canterbury's reasonable-patient standard, capacity and consent for minors

stem:
Patient: 9-year-old girl
Brought by: her grandmother, who drives her to all her appointments
Family: her parents are divorced, and her mother has legal custody
Need: extraction of a nonrestorable primary molar; no swelling
Who can give valid consent for the extraction?
choices: Her grandmother, as the adult who brought her in today
The girl herself, as long as she agrees to it
No one: the dentist can proceed under implied consent
ex: Minors: a parent or legal guardian consents; others need legal authority or written authorization. An emancipated minor consents for themselves.
why: Bringing the child isn't legal authority unless she is a guardian or holds written authorization from the parent.
A child's assent is sought, but it doesn't replace a parent's consent.
A parent or legal guardian consents for a minor; here, the mother with legal custody.
Implied consent covers emergencies, and this isn't one.

stem: True or false: A signed consent form is valid informed consent even if the patient didn't understand the explanation.
ex: The form documents the consent discussion; it isn't the consent. Valid consent needs understanding and a voluntary choice by a patient with capacity.
why: The form only documents consent; valid consent needs understanding and a voluntary choice by a patient with capacity.
Without understanding there is no informed consent, signature or not.

stem:
Patient: 38-year-old woman, new to the practice
Chief complaint: "I want a crown on my back tooth."
Findings: a large, failing restoration on #19 and possible caries on several teeth
She refuses all radiographs because she doesn't want the radiation, and offers to sign a waiver.
What is the most appropriate course?
choices: Accept her signed waiver as protection, then prepare the crown on #19 without taking any radiographs
Explain the risks of refusing, document her refusal, and decline care that can't meet the standard
Take the radiographs anyway, since they are clearly in her best interest
Dismiss her from the practice before any examination is done
ex: Informed refusal: explain the consequences, document and have it signed. Patients may refuse, but may not demand treatment inconsistent with the standard of care.
why: A waiver doesn't release the dentist from the standard of care, and a crown can't be planned safely without seeing the tooth.
Refusal is her right, but she can't require care below the standard of care; a waiver doesn't release the dentist from it.
Treating a competent adult against her refusal violates her autonomy.
Nothing requires ending the relationship; once she understands why they're needed, she may accept the radiographs.

stem: Each of the following is one of the abilities a patient needs for decision-making capacity EXCEPT:
choices: Appreciating that the information applies to their own situation
Reasoning about the options and their consequences
Expressing a clear and consistent choice
ex: Capacity (a clinical judgment): understand, appreciate, reason, express a choice. Competence is a legal finding by a court.
why: One of the four abilities: understanding.
One of the four abilities: appreciation.
One of the four abilities: reasoning.
One of the four abilities: expressing a choice.
A patient with capacity may disagree; refusing a recommendation isn't proof of incapacity.

stem: Which statement about HIPAA's Privacy Rule is true?
choices: A dentist may send a patient's records to the oral surgeon she refers him to without a separate written authorization
The Privacy Rule protects electronic records but not paper charts or spoken information
A patient has no right under HIPAA to see or get a copy of his own dental record
The minimum necessary standard means radiographs must be withheld when a patient is referred to a specialist for treatment
ex: HIPAA: PHI in any form; no authorization needed for treatment, payment, operations or legally required reports; patients may access and copy their records.
why: Disclosures for treatment, payment and health care operations don't need the patient's written authorization.
Protected health information is covered in any form: spoken, paper or electronic.
Patients have the right to see and get a copy, generally within 30 days.
Minimum necessary doesn't apply to disclosures to another provider for treatment.

likely.t: Confidentiality, HIPAA and the duty to warn

stem: Which action by a member of the dental team violates HIPAA?
choices: Calling a patient's insurance company to verify her dental benefits before her treatment begins
Sending a patient's radiographs to the endodontist who is treating him
Reporting suspected child abuse to child protective services
Telling a coworker who isn't involved in a patient's care about the patient's HIV status
ex: Need to know: PHI goes to those caring for the patient or handling payment and operations, and where the law requires it.
why: Sharing PHI for payment is allowed without authorization.
Sharing for treatment is allowed without authorization.
Disclosures required by law, such as abuse reports, are allowed.
Sharing PHI with someone who has no treatment, payment or operations need for it is an impermissible disclosure.

stem: True or false: The Tarasoff case held that a clinician can have a duty to protect an identifiable person whom a patient has seriously threatened, even though it means breaking confidentiality.
ex: Tarasoff (1976): the protective privilege ends where the public peril begins. The risk of an unnecessary warning is a reasonable price for the lives it may save.
why: The court held that an identifiable person at serious risk must be protected or warned.
The statement is right: Tarasoff set the duty to warn or protect.

stem:
Patient: 4-year-old boy
Brought by: his mother, who says he "fell off the couch"
Findings: bruises of different colors on both cheeks and the left ear, a torn maxillary labial frenum, and several untreated carious teeth
History: the mother's account of the fall changes when you ask again
What should the dentist do?
choices: Wait until the next visit to see whether new injuries appear
Report the suspected abuse to child protective services
Confront the mother about abuse before deciding anything
Mention the bruises to the boy's pediatrician and take no other action
Document the findings, but report only once abuse can be proven
ex: Bruises in different stages of healing on the face and ears, a torn frenum, a changing story and neglected caries all point to abuse and neglect: report to child protective services or the police.
why: Waiting leaves the child at risk; the duty is triggered by suspicion.
A reasonable suspicion is enough: dentists are mandated reporters, and good-faith reports are protected.
Confronting the caregiver can put the child at more risk; report to the authorities.
Telling another clinician doesn't meet the legal duty to report.
Proof isn't required; a reasonable suspicion triggers the report.

likely.t: Reporting suspected child abuse and neglect

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. A dentist should be certain that injuries were caused on purpose before reporting suspected child abuse.
2. A dentist who reports suspected abuse in good faith is protected from liability even when abuse is not confirmed.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: The legal threshold is a reasonable suspicion; investigating is the authorities' job. Every state grants good-faith reporters immunity, and in most states failing to report is an offense.
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: a reasonable suspicion is enough; investigating is the authorities' job.
Statement 2 is true, not false: every state grants good-faith reporters immunity.
Statement 1 is false, not true: a reasonable suspicion is enough; investigating is the authorities' job. Statement 2 is true, not false: every state grants good-faith reporters immunity.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. The risk of HIV infection after a needlestick from an HIV-infected source is about 30%.
2. Dental staff with occupational exposure must be offered a hepatitis C vaccine.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: After a needlestick from an infected source: HBV about 30%, HCV about 2%, HIV about 0.3%. Only HBV has a vaccine, and OSHA requires employers to offer it free.
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: the HIV risk is about 0.3%; about 30% is hepatitis B's risk. Statement 2 is false, not true: there is no hepatitis C vaccine; OSHA requires the hepatitis B vaccine to be offered free.
Statement 1 is false: the HIV risk is about 0.3%; about 30% is hepatitis B's risk. Statement 2 is false: there is no hepatitis C vaccine; OSHA requires the hepatitis B vaccine to be offered free.
Statement 1 is false, not true: the HIV risk is about 0.3%; about 30% is hepatitis B's risk.

stem: A dental student sticks her finger with a used anesthetic needle after injecting a patient whose medical history lists HIV. What should she do first?
choices: Squeeze the wound to make it bleed, then soak her finger in bleach
Finish the appointment, then report the exposure at the end of the day
Wash the wound with soap and water and report the exposure right away
Wait for the patient's latest viral load before taking any action at all
ex: After an exposure: wash (flush eyes or mouth with water), report immediately, evaluate the source with consent; HIV prophylaxis ideally within 2 hours and no later than 72.
why: Squeezing and caustic agents aren't recommended; they can damage the tissue.
Prophylaxis works best started as soon as possible, ideally within 2 hours.
Wash first, then report at once so the source can be tested and HIV prophylaxis started, ideally within 2 hours.
Washing and reporting can't wait; testing and the prophylaxis decision follow the report.

likely.t: Bloodborne pathogens: transmission risks, the steps after a needlestick, and OSHA's hepatitis B vaccine rule

stem: True or false: Under OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, an employer must offer the hepatitis B vaccine free to employees with occupational exposure, and an employee who declines signs a declination.
ex: The vaccine is offered at no cost within 10 working days of assignment; an employee who refuses signs a declination and can still get the vaccine later.
why: The vaccine is offered at no cost within 10 working days of assignment, and a refusal is documented with a signed declination.
The statement is right on both points.

stem:
Which statements about arguments are true?
1. Modus ponens (if p then q; p; so q) is a valid form of argument.
2. Affirming the consequent (if p then q; q; so p) is a valid form of argument.
3. A valid deductive argument whose premises are all true is sound.
4. Whether an argument is valid depends on whether its premises are true.
ex: Validity is a matter of structure; soundness adds true premises. Modus ponens and modus tollens are valid; affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are invalid.
why: It leaves out 3, which is true: sound means valid with true premises.
It includes 2, which is false: affirming the consequent is invalid, because q can be true for other reasons. It leaves out 3, which is true: sound means valid with true premises.
It includes 2, which is false: affirming the consequent is invalid, because q can be true for other reasons.

Statements 1 and 3 are true. Statement 2 is false: affirming the consequent is invalid, because q can be true for other reasons. Statement 4 is false: validity is about structure alone; the truth of the premises decides soundness.

likely.t: Arguments, fallacies and moral theories

stem: In a clinic meeting, a colleague argues: "If we let parents refuse fluoride varnish, they'll soon refuse every preventive service, and our clinic will be full of children with rampant caries." What fallacy is this?
ex: The five fallacies from the class notes: straw man, ad hominem, appeal to ignorance, begging the question and slippery slope.
why: A straw man misstates someone's view to attack it; here the claim is a chain of predicted consequences.
Ad hominem rejects a claim because of who made it.
It claims one step will inevitably lead, step by step, to a dire outcome.
Begging the question uses the conclusion as its own premise.
Appeal to ignorance argues from a lack of proof.

stem: A dentist separates a file in a canal. She decides she must tell the patient, reasoning that hiding it to protect her reputation would treat him merely as a means, whatever the consequences of telling. Which theory is she using?
ex: Deontology judges acts by duty and motive (Kant: universalizable maxims; persons as ends). Utilitarianism judges by consequences.
why: A utilitarian would decide by weighing the consequences of telling against those of not telling.
Care ethics centers on relationships and responsibilities to particular people.
Casuistry reasons from comparable cases rather than from a universal rule.
Treating people as ends and never merely as means is Kant's second formulation of the categorical imperative; consequences don't decide it.

stem: Which statement about dental records is false?
choices: An error in a paper chart is corrected with a single line, dated and initialed, so the original stays readable
After a complaint, a dentist may rewrite an old entry to make it more complete, as long as it keeps its original date
The medical history should be reviewed with the patient at every visit
The dentist owns the original record, and the patient is entitled to a copy
ex: The record is a legal document: never erase, alter or backdate; correct with a single line or a dated addendum.
why: This is true: the original entry must stay legible.
This is the false one: altering or backdating a record is unethical and can be illegal. Add a new entry dated the day it is written.
This is true: medications and conditions change; review it each visit and update it fully at least yearly.
This is true: originals stay with the practice, and copies go to the patient on request.

stem: A dentist wants to know whether a new desensitizing varnish works better than her usual one. She has framed a PICO question and searched TRIP, which turned up three randomized trials. In the 5 A's, what is her next step?
choices: Apply the trials' findings with her next patient who has sensitivity
Assess how well the new varnish has worked in her own patients
Appraise the trials' design, validity and results
Ask a new clinical question built on the trials' conclusions
ex: The 5 A's run ask, acquire, appraise, apply, assess. Having acquired the evidence, she appraises it next.
why: Apply comes after appraise; using evidence she hasn't judged skips a step.
Assess is the last step, looking back after the evidence has been applied.
Appraise follows acquire: she judges whether the trials are valid and their results important before using them.
Ask is the first step, already done when she framed her PICO question.

likely.t: The 5 A's in order and building a PICO(T) question; question types and their best designs

stem:
Patient: 9-year-old girl
Chief complaint: recall visit; her mother asks about sealants
History: three restorations in the past year; high caries risk
Findings: sound, deep pits and fissures on the first permanent molars
Her mother asks: "Would sealants protect her molars better than the fluoride varnish alone over the next two years?"
In the PICO question built from this visit, what is C?
choices: Sealants on the first permanent molars
Children at high risk of caries
New occlusal caries over the next two years
ex: P: children at high caries risk; I: sealants; C: fluoride varnish alone; O: new caries on the molars; T: two years.
why: That is I, the intervention being asked about.
The comparison is the alternative the intervention is measured against: varnish without sealants.
That is P, the patient or population.
That is O, with T (two years) attached.

stem: True or false: A background question, such as "What causes dry socket?", is best written in PICO format.
ex: Background questions (who, what, when, why, how about one condition) don't need PICO; a textbook or review answers them. PICO is built for foreground questions, which compare at least two options for a specific patient or problem.
why: Background questions ask for general facts about one condition; PICO is for foreground questions that compare options for a patient.
A textbook or review answers a background question; PICO fits foreground questions that compare two or more options.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. The lecture's search order is the TRIP database first, then PubMed Clinical Queries, then the Cochrane Library.
2. PubMed Clinical Queries filters results by the type of question: therapy, diagnosis, etiology or prognosis.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Start with TRIP, which returns guidelines, reviews and primary studies at once; then PubMed's Clinical Queries, which filters by question type; then the Cochrane Library's systematic reviews.
why: Statement 1 is true: the class guide lists TRIP first, then PubMed Clinical Queries, then Cochrane. Statement 2 is true: Clinical Queries narrows a PubMed search to studies suited to the question type and finds systematic reviews.

Statement 1 is true, not false: the class guide lists TRIP first, then PubMed Clinical Queries, then Cochrane. Statement 2 is true, not false: Clinical Queries narrows a PubMed search to studies suited to the question type and finds systematic reviews.
Statement 2 is true, not false: Clinical Queries narrows a PubMed search to studies suited to the question type and finds systematic reviews.
Statement 1 is true, not false: the class guide lists TRIP first, then PubMed Clinical Queries, then Cochrane.

stem: At a county health fair, researchers examine 1,200 adults once for untreated caries and, at the same visit, ask how many sugary drinks they have a day. They find more caries among heavy soda drinkers. What is the design?
ex: One visit, with exposure and outcome measured together in each person: cross-sectional. It shows prevalence and an association, but not which came first.
why: A case-control study would start with people who have caries and people who don't, then look back at past exposure.
A cohort follows people over time; here everyone was seen once.
An ecological study compares group averages (cities, countries), not individuals.
Exposure (soda) and outcome (caries) are measured at the same time in the same people: a snapshot.

likely.t: Naming the design from a study description, and what case-control and cohort studies are each good for

stem: Investigators enroll 300 patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma and 300 patients without it, then interview both groups about their past tobacco use, alcohol use and diet. Which design is this, and which measure of association does it report?
ex: Cases with the disease and controls without, compared for past exposures: case-control. It suits rare diseases with long latency and several risk factors at once, and reports an odds ratio. Watch for recall bias.
why: Without following exposed people forward, a case-control study can't compute incidence, so it can't give a relative risk.
A cohort starts with the exposure and follows people for the outcome; this study starts with the outcome.
A retrospective cohort still groups people by past exposure, not by disease, and gives a relative risk.
A cross-sectional study measures a population at one time; it doesn't choose people by whether they have the disease.
It starts with the outcome (cancer or not) and looks back at exposures, so it reports an odds ratio.

likely.t: Naming the design from a study description, and what case-control and cohort studies are each good for

stem: Researchers record the daily brushing habits of 500 adults aged 30–60 with a healthy periodontium and examine them again five years later for periodontitis. Compared with a case-control study, what can this design do?
choices: Show that the habit came before the disease, and compute incidence
Study a rare disease efficiently with a small sample of participants
Avoid losing any participants to follow-up over the five years
Prove cause and effect as firmly as a randomized controlled trial
